And §8.2.4 on Bayesian additive regression trees is not covered in the lectures; it is readable as extension material once boosting is understood, since BART is essentially a Bayesian treatment of the same additive-tree idea.

title: Trees, forests and boosting
text:
Where this leads
The methods of this chapter produce models that predict well and explain little. That is a genuine change in what a statistical model is for, and it is worth stating plainly. A fitted random forest supports the claim that herb cover can be predicted from these four variables to within a certain error. It does not support a claim about the effect of raising soil pH by one unit, and no amount of variable-importance plotting converts it into one.


KEY — Prediction and explanation are different goals served by different models.
The course began with one proposition: statistics arises the moment a complicated process is described with a simple model. Every method since has been a version of it. Each approximates a process, explains part of the variation, leaves a residual, spends some measure of flexibility, and must be judged on data it has not seen.




↪ Day 11 returns to the thousands of genes of Day 2, and asks a different question: not which single genes change, but which sets of genes change together.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
text:
From genes to gene sets
Day 2 left a bioinformatician with thousands of p-values, one per gene, and a correction for multiple testing. That answers the question which genes change? It often answers it badly. The changes may be too small to survive the correction, or the list may be long and without a common theme. And studies of the same biology often produce lists that hardly overlap.
This chapter changes the question to which groups of genes change together? The groups are gene sets: genes that share a function, a pathway or a location. Two families of methods answer the question. Over-representation analysis counts how many genes of a set are on a list of significant genes. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) uses the whole ranked list of genes, without a threshold, and borrows its test statistic from the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test.
Both are built from ideas met earlier in the course: counts and their distributions (Day 1), multiple testing and the difference between confirming and exploring (Day 2), and resampling (Day 7). The chapter uses simulated genes and gene sets, so that the truth is known.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
text:
Why lists of single genes disappoint
The paper that introduced GSEA (Subramanian et al. 2005) gave four reasons to look beyond single genes. After correcting for multiple testing, no gene may be significant, because the biological effects are modest compared with the noise. Alternatively, the list may be long, with no unifying theme, and its interpretation then depends on the expertise of whoever reads it. Cellular processes involve sets of genes acting together: a modest increase in every gene of a pathway can matter more than a large increase in one gene. And different groups studying the same system often obtain lists of significant genes with distressingly little overlap.
The last point is easy to reproduce. Three laboratories study the same biology: 300 of 5,000 genes truly change, all by the same moderate amount. Each laboratory measures four treated and four control samples and reports its 300 most significant genes.


Code for the figure
set.seed(3)
G <- 5000; truly_changed <- 1:300; n <- 4; grp <- rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), each = n)
top <- lapply(1:3, function(s) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(G * 2 * n), G)
  X[truly_changed, grp] <- X[truly_changed, grp] + 1.2
  p <- 2 * pt(-abs(row_t(X, grp)), 2 * n - 2)
  order(p)[1:300]
})
A <- top[[1]]; B <- top[[2]]; C <- top[[3]]
region <- c(A = length(setdiff(A, union(B, C))), B = length(setdiff(B, union(A, C))),
            C = length(setdiff(C, union(A, B))),
            AB = length(setdiff(intersect(A, B), C)), AC = length(setdiff(intersect(A, C), B)),
            BC = length(setdiff(intersect(B, C), A)), ABC = length(Reduce(intersect, top)))
circ <- function(x, y, r, col) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200); lines(x + r * cos(t), y + r * sin(t), col = col, lwd = 3)
}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(-3.3, 3.3), ylim = c(-3, 3.2), asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
circ(-0.9, 0.6, 1.8, col_orange); circ(0.9, 0.6, 1.8, col_blue); circ(0, -0.9, 1.8, col_green)
text(c(-1.6, 1.6, 0, 0, -0.95, 0.95, 0), c(1.1, 1.1, -1.9, 1.25, -0.35, -0.35, 0.15),
     region[c("A", "B", "C", "AB", "AC", "BC", "ABC")], cex = 1.3, font = 2)
text(c(-2.4, 2.4, 0), c(2.6, 2.6, -2.95), c("study 1", "study 2", "study 3"),
     col = c(col_orange, col_blue, col_green), cex = 1.1, font = 2)








Figure 13.1: The 300 most significant genes in three simulated studies of the same biology. Each study finds about 80 of the 300 truly changed genes, but different ones: two lists share only about 30 genes, and all three share a handful. The real figure, from three published studies of stem cells, looks much the same (Fortunel et al. 2003).






c(true_genes_in_each_list = round(mean(sapply(top, function(t) sum(t %in% truly_changed)))),
  overlap_study_1_and_2 = length(intersect(A, B)))

#> true_genes_in_each_list   overlap_study_1_and_2 
#>                      81                      31


Every list is mostly right in the sense that matters: the genes on it are much more likely than chance to be truly changed. But with small effects and few samples, which of the 300 changed genes make it into the top 300 is largely a matter of luck. A conclusion about a group of genes, such as “the genes of this pathway go up”, can be stable even when the individual lists are not.


KEY — With modest effects and few samples, individual gene lists are unstable. Questions about groups of genes can be answered more reliably.


Where gene sets come from: Gene Ontology and pathways
A gene set is any group of genes defined before the experiment. The most widely used source is the Gene Ontology (GO) (Ashburner et al. 2000), which describes genes in three vocabularies: the biological processes they take part in, their molecular functions, and the cellular components where they act. The terms are organised as a directed acyclic graph: a specific term is linked to more general terms by relations such as is a, part of and regulates.


Code for the figure
nodes <- data.frame(
  id = c("GO:0008150", "GO:0009987", "GO:0065007", "GO:0016043", "GO:0050789",
         "GO:0030030", "GO:0050794", "GO:0031344"),
  label = c("biological_process", "cellular process", "biological regulation",
            "cellular component\norganization", "regulation of\nbiological process",
            "cell projection\norganization", "regulation of\ncellular process",
            "regulation of cell\nprojection organization"),
  x = c(0, -2.2, 2.2, -3, 2.2, -3, 0.6, -0.8),
  y = c(4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0))
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("GO:0009987", "GO:0065007", "GO:0016043", "GO:0050789", "GO:0030030",
           "GO:0050794", "GO:0050794", "GO:0031344", "GO:0031344"),
  to   = c("GO:0008150", "GO:0008150", "GO:0009987", "GO:0065007", "GO:0016043",
           "GO:0050789", "GO:0009987", "GO:0050794", "GO:0030030"),
  type = c("is_a", "is_a", "is_a", "is_a", "is_a", "is_a", "regulates", "is_a", "regulates"))
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(-4.3, 3.6), ylim = c(-0.5, 4.5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
pos <- function(id) unlist(nodes[nodes$id == id, c("x", "y")])
for (k in seq_len(nrow(edges))) {
  a <- pos(edges$from[k]); b <- pos(edges$to[k])
  arrows(a[1], a[2] + 0.28, b[1], b[2] - 0.3, length = 0.09, lwd = 2,
         col = ifelse(edges$type[k] == "is_a", "grey55", col_orange))
}
for (k in seq_len(nrow(nodes))) {
  rect(nodes$x[k] - 0.85, nodes$y[k] - 0.28, nodes$x[k] + 0.85, nodes$y[k] + 0.28,
       col = "white", border = "grey30")
  text(nodes$x[k], nodes$y[k] + 0.08, nodes$label[k], cex = 0.68)
  text(nodes$x[k], nodes$y[k] - 0.2, nodes$id[k], cex = 0.55, col = col_grey)
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("grey55", col_orange),
       legend = c("is a", "regulates"), cex = 0.85)








Figure 13.2: A small part of the Gene Ontology. Arrows point from a specific term to a more general one; grey arrows mean is a, orange arrows regulates. A gene annotated to a specific term is counted in all the terms above it, so gene sets are nested and overlap.





Pathway databases such as KEGG and Reactome provide another source, and collections such as MSigDB bundle sets from many sources. For statistics, three properties of these sets matter more than their biology:

Sets overlap and are nested. A gene annotated to a specific GO term also counts for every term above it. Tests for different sets are therefore not independent.
Set sizes vary from a handful of genes to thousands. A test statistic must be comparable across sizes.
Annotation is incomplete and biased. Well-studied genes carry many annotations, poorly studied genes few. Sets reflect what is known, not only what is true.



⚠ The gene sets must be chosen before looking at the results. Choosing the sets that “look interesting” after the analysis is the double dipping of Day 2.

↪ Real analyses read the sets from GO, KEGG or MSigDB with Bioconductor packages such as clusterProfiler or fgsea. The statistics underneath are the ones in this chapter.







CautionCheck yourself



A gene set for “cellular process” contains thousands of genes, one for “regulation of cell projection organization” a few dozen. Why are the two tests not independent, and why can a significant result for the large set be uninformative?






TipAnswer





Every gene annotated to the specific term is also annotated to the general term above it, so the two sets share genes, and a change in those genes affects both tests. A very large set is significant as soon as a small fraction of its genes change; the result then says little more than “something happens in the cell”. Specific sets are usually more informative, even though they have less power.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
text:
Over-representation analysis

A two-by-two table
The oldest form of enrichment analysis starts from a list of significant genes, for example those with a false discovery rate below 5%. It asks whether the genes of a set are over-represented on the list. Every gene of the universe, the genes that could have appeared on the list, falls into one of four cells:




in the set
not in the set
total




on the list
\(x\)
\(k - x\)
\(k\)


not on the list
\(m - x\)

\(N - k\)


total
\(m\)
\(N - m\)
\(N\)



If the list has nothing to do with the set, the \(k\) genes on the list are like \(k\) balls drawn without replacement from an urn with \(m\) marked balls among \(N\). The number of marked balls drawn then has a hypergeometric distribution, with expected value \(k\,m/N\), and the p-value is the probability of an overlap at least as large as the observed one:
\[P(X \ge x) = \sum_{j \ge x} \frac{\binom{m}{j}\binom{N - m}{k - j}}{\binom{N}{k}} .\]
This is the one-sided version of Fisher’s exact test for a \(2 \times 2\) table.


DEF — The hypergeometric distribution counts marked items in a sample drawn without replacement. The binomial of Day 1 is the same count with replacement, and is a good approximation when the universe is large.

set.seed(11)
N_genes   <- 10000
expressed <- sort(sample(N_genes, 5000))          # genes measured in this tissue
set_genes <- c(sample(expressed, 190), sample(setdiff(1:N_genes, expressed), 10))

# a list of 800 significant genes: 40 genes of the set changed, plus 760 others
# drawn at random from the remaining expressed genes
changed <- sample(intersect(set_genes, expressed), 40)
de_list <- c(changed, sample(setdiff(expressed, changed), 760))

universe <- expressed
tab <- table(on_list = factor(universe %in% de_list, c(TRUE, FALSE)),
             in_set  = factor(universe %in% set_genes, c(TRUE, FALSE)))
tab

#>        in_set
#> on_list TRUE FALSE
#>   TRUE    55   745
#>   FALSE  135  4065

x <- tab["TRUE", "TRUE"]; m <- sum(universe %in% set_genes); k <- length(de_list)
k * m / length(universe)                     # expected overlap

#> [1] 30.4

c(hypergeometric = phyper(x - 1, m, length(universe) - m, k, lower.tail = FALSE),
  fisher         = fisher.test(tab, alternative = "greater")$p.value)

#> hypergeometric         fisher 
#>   3.253917e-06   3.253917e-06


The set contributes 55 genes to the list where about 30 are expected, and both calculations give the same, very small p-value.


The universe matters
The universe is the step most often done wrong. In the example, only the 5,000 genes expressed in the tissue could ever appear on the list, and almost all genes of the set are among them. Suppose now that the list contains no enrichment at all, 800 expressed genes drawn at random, and the analysis is run with the whole genome as universe.

set.seed(12)
random_list <- sample(expressed, 800)                       # no enrichment at all
ora_p <- function(list, universe) {
  tab <- table(factor(universe %in% list, c(TRUE, FALSE)),
               factor(universe %in% set_genes, c(TRUE, FALSE)))
  c(overlap = tab[1, 1], expected = round(length(list) * mean(universe %in% set_genes), 1),
    p = signif(fisher.test(tab, alternative = "greater")$p.value, 3))
}
rbind(whole_genome    = ora_p(random_list, 1:N_genes),
      expressed_genes = ora_p(random_list, expressed))

#>                 overlap expected        p
#> whole_genome         32     16.0 0.000114
#> expressed_genes      32     30.4 0.404000


With the genome as universe, the set appears strongly enriched: its genes are expressed, and expressed genes are the only ones that can be on a list. The correct universe removes the artefact.


KEY — The universe is the set of genes that could have been on the list: the genes that were measured, expressed and kept after filtering. A universe that is too large produces enrichment from nothing.


What over-representation analysis assumes
Two further weaknesses follow from the urn model.

The threshold. The list depends on an arbitrary cut-off (FDR 5%, or the top 500). Genes just below the cut-off count as much as genes that did not change at all, and a different cut-off can change the conclusion.
Independence. The urn assumes that genes are drawn independently. Genes in a pathway are co-regulated, so they tend to be on the list together or not at all. The effective number of independent draws is smaller than the count suggests, and the p-values are too small.

GSEA addresses the first weakness directly. The second returns below.






CautionCheck yourself



An over-representation analysis of a liver experiment uses all 20,000 human protein-coding genes as universe. Which kind of gene set is most likely to come out as falsely enriched, and how would you choose the universe instead?






TipAnswer





Sets of genes that are specifically expressed in the liver, or more generally in the measured tissue: their genes are over-represented among the measured, expressed genes, and therefore among any list of significant genes, whatever the treatment does. The universe should be the genes that could have been called significant: those measured on the platform, expressed in the tissue and retained after the filtering step of the differential-expression analysis.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
section: Distributions of p-values, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test
text:
Distributions of p-values, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test
GSEA does not use a list but the whole distribution of gene-level results. Its statistic descends from a classical test for comparing distributions, which is easiest to introduce with p-values.

p-values under the null and the alternative
If a test statistic \(T\) has a continuous distribution function \(F\) under \(H_0\), the p-value \(P = 1 - F(T)\) (or its two-sided version) is uniformly distributed between 0 and 1 when \(H_0\) is true:
\[P(P \le p) = P\big(T \ge F^{-1}(1-p)\big) = 1 - F\big(F^{-1}(1-p)\big) = p .\]
The figure repeats a one-sample t-test 10,000 times on samples of 15 observations with true mean 2. On the left the null hypothesis is the truth (\(\mu_0 = 2\)); on the right it is not (\(\mu_0 = 1.75\)).


Code for the figure
set.seed(568)
Xp <- matrix(rnorm(10000 * 15, 2, 1.5), 10000)
t_stat <- function(mu0) (rowMeans(Xp) - mu0) / (apply(Xp, 1, sd) / sqrt(15))
p_null <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat(2)), 14)
p_alt  <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat(1.75)), 14)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (k in 1:2) {
  p <- list(p_null, p_alt)[[k]]
  hist(p, breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), col = c(col_orange, rep("#DCE6F1", 19)), border = "grey50",
       las = 1, ylim = c(0, 1100), xlab = "p-value", ylab = "number of tests",
       main = c("H0 true: effect size 0", "H0 false: effect size 1/6")[k])
  abline(h = 500, lty = 2, col = col_blue)
}








Figure 13.3: p-values of 10,000 one-sample t-tests. Left: the null hypothesis is true, and the p-values are uniform; about 5% fall below 0.05 (orange). Right: the true mean differs from the null value by a sixth of a standard deviation, and the p-values pile up near zero.







Comparing distributions: the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic
To compare the two histograms with the uniform distribution formally, plot their empirical cumulative distribution functions (ECDFs): for each value \(x\), the fraction of p-values at or below \(x\). Under \(H_0\) the ECDF follows the diagonal. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic is the largest vertical distance between an ECDF \(F_n\) and the reference distribution \(F\):
\[D_n = \sup_x \big|F_n(x) - F(x)\big| .\]


Code for the figure
xs <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1001)
F_alt <- ecdf(p_alt)(xs); F_null <- ecdf(p_null)(xs)
k_max <- which.max(abs(F_alt - xs))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(xs, F_alt, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = col_blue, las = 1, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "p-value", ylab = "fraction of p-values at or below")
lines(xs, F_null, lwd = 3, col = col_green)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
segments(xs[k_max], xs[k_max], xs[k_max], F_alt[k_max], col = col_orange, lwd = 4)
text(xs[k_max], (xs[k_max] + F_alt[k_max]) / 2, "D", pos = 4, col = col_orange, font = 2)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 3, col = c(col_blue, col_green),
       legend = c("H0 false", "H0 true"))








Figure 13.4: Empirical cumulative distribution functions of the two sets of p-values, and the uniform distribution (dashed diagonal). The orange segment marks the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic D for the p-values under the alternative: the largest vertical distance to the diagonal.






ks.test(p_alt, "punif")

#> 
#>  Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
#> 
#> data:  p_alt
#> D = 0.09794, p-value < 2.2e-16
#> alternative hypothesis: two-sided

c(critical_value_one_sample = 1.358 / sqrt(length(p_alt)))

#> critical_value_one_sample 
#>                   0.01358


For a sample of size \(n\) compared with a fixed distribution, \(D_n\) exceeds \(c(\alpha)/\sqrt n\) with probability \(\alpha\) under \(H_0\), where \(c(0.05) = 1.358\) and \(c(0.01) = 1.628\). Here \(D\) is about 0.10, far above the critical value of 0.014. When two samples of sizes \(n\) and \(m\) are compared with each other, ks.test(sample1, sample2), the critical value becomes \(c(\alpha)\sqrt{(n + m)/(nm)}\).


KEY — The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test asks whether a sample is distributed like a reference. GSEA asks the same question of a gene set: are its genes distributed over the ranked list like randomly chosen genes?

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
text:
Gene set enrichment analysis

Ranking all genes
GSEA starts from a statistic for every gene, here the t-statistic comparing two groups, and ranks all genes from most up-regulated to most down-regulated. No threshold is applied. The simulated experiment has 2,000 genes, measured in 8 control and 8 treated samples, and three gene sets of 40 genes each:

S1: every gene is raised by 0.8 standard deviations in the treated samples, a modest change that few genes would survive alone;
S2: a random set, with no change;
S3: no change either, but its genes are strongly correlated: they share a common source of variation between samples, as co-regulated genes do.


set.seed(2027)
G <- 2000; n <- 8; grp <- rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), each = n)
X <- matrix(rnorm(G * 2 * n), G)
sets <- list(S1 = 1:40, S2 = 41:80, S3 = 81:120)
X[sets$S1, grp] <- X[sets$S1, grp] + 0.8                   # a real, modest shift
shared <- rnorm(2 * n)                                     # a common factor per sample
X[sets$S3, ] <- X[sets$S3, ] + matrix(1.2 * shared, 40, 2 * n, byrow = TRUE)

t_obs <- row_t(X, grp)
p_gene <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_obs), 2 * n - 2)
c(S1_genes_significant_after_BH = sum(p.adjust(p_gene, "BH")[sets$S1] < 0.05))

#> S1_genes_significant_after_BH 
#>                             0


Not one of the 40 genes of S1 is significant on its own after the Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The question is whether the set, taken together, is.


The running sum and the enrichment score
Walk down the ranked list. Each time a gene of the set is met, a running sum goes up; each time another gene is met, it goes down. In the formulation of Subramanian et al. (2005), after the first \(i\) genes of the list,
\[P_\text{hit}(S, i) = \sum_{g_j \in S,\ j \le i} \frac{|r_j|^p}{N_R},
\qquad
P_\text{miss}(S, i) = \sum_{g_j \notin S,\ j \le i} \frac{1}{N - N_S},
\qquad
N_R = \sum_{g_j \in S} |r_j|^p ,\]
where \(r_j\) is the statistic of the gene at rank \(j\), \(N\) the number of genes and \(N_S\) the size of the set. The enrichment score is the maximum deviation of \(P_\text{hit} - P_\text{miss}\) from zero.
With \(p = 0\) every hit counts equally, and the running sum is, up to scaling, the difference between the ECDF of the set’s ranks and that of all other genes: the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic. With \(p = 1\), the usual choice, genes with large statistics count more, so a set whose genes cluster in the middle of the list cannot reach a large score.

running_sum <- function(stat, in_set, p = 1) {
  o <- order(stat, decreasing = TRUE)
  hit  <- in_set[o]
  w    <- abs(stat[o])^p * hit
  cumsum(w) / sum(w) - cumsum(!hit) / sum(!hit)
}
enrichment_score <- function(stat, in_set, p = 1) {
  r <- running_sum(stat, in_set, p); r[which.max(abs(r))]
}
in_set <- lapply(sets, function(s) seq_len(G) %in% s)
es_obs <- sapply(in_set, function(s) enrichment_score(t_obs, s))
round(es_obs, 3)

#>     S1     S2     S3 
#>  0.728 -0.226 -0.569




Code for the figure
cols <- c(S1 = col_orange, S2 = col_blue, S3 = col_green)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (s in names(sets)) {
  r <- running_sum(t_obs, in_set[[s]])
  ranks <- which(in_set[[s]][order(t_obs, decreasing = TRUE)])
  plot(r, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = cols[s], las = 1, ylim = c(-0.85, 0.95),
       xlab = "rank in the list", ylab = "running enrichment score", main = s)
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  segments(ranks, 0.8, ranks, 0.92, col = cols[s])
  k <- which.max(abs(r)); points(k, r[k], pch = 19, col = cols[s], cex = 1.3)
}








Figure 13.5: Running sums for the three gene sets along the ranked list (rank 1 is the most up-regulated gene). The bars at the top mark where the genes of the set fall. S1’s genes cluster at the top, and the running sum climbs steeply. S2’s genes are spread evenly, and the sum wanders around zero. S3’s genes also cluster, at the bottom in this sample, although nothing changed: they are correlated and moved together by chance.







Significance by permutation
The enrichment score has no simple null distribution: it depends on the set size, on the weights, and on the correlation between genes. GSEA therefore obtains its null distribution by permutation. The labels of the samples (control or treated) are shuffled, all gene statistics are recomputed, and the enrichment score of each set is calculated again. Repeating this a thousand times gives the distribution of the score when the treatment has no effect; the p-value is the fraction of permutation scores at least as extreme as the observed one.

set.seed(1)
B <- 1000
es_null <- replicate(B, {
  t_perm <- row_t(X, sample(grp))                 # shuffle samples, keep genes together
  sapply(in_set, function(s) enrichment_score(t_perm, s))
})
p_sample_perm <- sapply(names(sets), function(s) mean(abs(es_null[s, ]) >= abs(es_obs[s])))
round(p_sample_perm, 3)

#>    S1    S2    S3 
#> 0.000 0.756 0.480


Set sizes differ between real gene sets, and so do their null distributions. GSEA therefore divides each score by the mean of the permutation scores of the same sign, giving a normalised enrichment score (NES) that can be compared across sets. With many sets, the p-values (or NES-based FDR values) are corrected for multiple testing, exactly as for genes on Day 2.


↪ Permutation is resampling without replacement, the sibling of the bootstrap (Day 7). Both replace a theoretical distribution by one built from the data themselves.


Permuting genes or permuting samples?
A cheaper alternative is to permute genes: draw random sets of 40 genes from the same ranked list, and compare their scores with the observed one. It needs only the one ranked list. But it treats the genes of a set as independent draws, and S3 shows what that costs.

set.seed(2)
es_gene_null <- replicate(B, enrichment_score(t_obs, seq_len(G) %in% sample(G, 40)))
p_gene_perm <- sapply(names(sets), function(s) mean(abs(es_gene_null) >= abs(es_obs[s])))
rbind(permute_samples = round(p_sample_perm, 3), permute_genes = round(p_gene_perm, 3))

#>                 S1    S2   S3
#> permute_samples  0 0.756 0.48
#> permute_genes    0 0.779 0.00




Code for the figure
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
hist(abs(es_null["S3", ]), breaks = 30, col = "#DCE6F1", border = "grey50", las = 1, xlim = c(0, 0.9),
     main = "permuting samples", xlab = "|enrichment score|", ylab = "permutations")
abline(v = abs(es_obs["S3"]), col = col_orange, lwd = 3)
hist(abs(es_gene_null), breaks = 30, col = "#DCE6F1", border = "grey50", las = 1, xlim = c(0, 0.9),
     main = "permuting genes", xlab = "|enrichment score|", ylab = "permutations")
abline(v = abs(es_obs["S3"]), col = col_orange, lwd = 3)








Figure 13.6: Null distributions for the enrichment score of S3, the correlated set without any real change, and its observed score (orange line). Permuting samples keeps the correlation between the set’s genes, so large scores are common and the observed score is unremarkable. Permuting genes breaks the correlation, so such a score looks impossible.





For S1 both approaches agree: the set is enriched. For S3 they disagree completely. Its genes moved together because they are correlated, not because of the treatment; sample permutation recognises this, gene permutation declares a discovery.
The two approaches test different null hypotheses (Goeman and Bühlmann 2007). A self-contained test asks whether the genes of the set are associated with the treatment at all; permuting samples answers it. A competitive test asks whether the set is more associated with the treatment than other genes are; permuting genes, and over-representation analysis, answer it, but only under the assumption that genes are independent. How often does that assumption fail? Repeated over 100 simulated experiments, each with a correlated set and no real change:

set.seed(3)
false_positive <- replicate(100, {
  Xs <- matrix(rnorm(1000 * 2 * n), 1000)
  Xs[1:40, ] <- Xs[1:40, ] + matrix(1.2 * rnorm(2 * n), 40, 2 * n, byrow = TRUE)
  s  <- seq_len(1000) <= 40
  ts <- row_t(Xs, grp); o <- enrichment_score(ts, s)
  null_s <- replicate(200, enrichment_score(row_t(Xs, sample(grp)), s))
  null_g <- replicate(200, enrichment_score(ts, seq_len(1000) %in% sample(1000, 40)))
  c(permute_samples = mean(abs(null_s) >= abs(o)) < 0.05,
    permute_genes   = mean(abs(null_g) >= abs(o)) < 0.05)
})
rowMeans(false_positive)          # fraction of experiments with p < 0.05

#> permute_samples   permute_genes 
#>            0.05            0.71


Sample permutation keeps the false-positive rate at the nominal 5%; gene permutation declares a correlated set enriched in most experiments.


KEY — Genes are not independent. Permuting samples keeps their correlation and gives valid p-values; permuting genes, and the urn model of over-representation analysis, ignore it and produce discoveries from co-regulation alone.

⚠ Sample permutation needs enough samples: with 3 against 3 there are only 20 distinct ways to split six samples, so the smallest attainable p-value is 0.05. This is one reason gene permutation is still used in practice, and one reason small studies should be interpreted with care.







CautionCheck yourself



A GSEA on an experiment with 4 treated and 4 control samples reports, for a set of 25 genes from one protein complex, a p-value of 0.0001 obtained by permuting genes. What would you check before believing it?






TipAnswer





Genes of one protein complex are typically co-regulated, so the set’s genes are correlated, and a gene-permutation p-value can be far too small, as for S3. Check the correlation between the set’s genes, and repeat the analysis with sample permutation (with 4 against 4 there are 70 splits, so the smallest possible p-value is about 0.014). Also check that the set was chosen before the analysis, and how many sets were tested: 0.0001 among thousands of sets is less impressive than it sounds.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
text:
Enrichment within the course
Gene set analysis brings together several threads of the course, and each carries a warning.

Confirming or exploring (Day 2). Testing a handful of sets chosen from the hypothesis, as the GSEA authors recommended, is confirmatory. Testing all 10,000 GO terms and reporting the top of the list is exploratory: the result is a hypothesis, and it needs correction for multiple testing and independent confirmation.
Design (Day 2). Batch effects shift many genes together, exactly like the shared factor of S3. An enrichment found in a confounded design is an enrichment of the batch.
Distributions (Day 1). The hypergeometric distribution is a count with a ceiling, like the binomial; the uniform distribution of p-values under the null is what the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test checks.
Resampling (Day 7). Permutation must respect the structure of the data: shuffle the units that were randomised (samples), not the units that are correlated (genes).

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
text:
Summary

Gene set analysis replaces the question which genes change? by which groups of genes change together? Group-level conclusions are often more stable than gene lists.
Gene sets come from GO and pathway databases; they overlap, vary in size and reflect what is known. They must be chosen before the results are seen.
Over-representation analysis uses a \(2 \times 2\) table and the hypergeometric distribution (Fisher’s exact test). It depends on a threshold, on the correct universe, and on the independence of genes.
GSEA ranks all genes and computes a running-sum enrichment score, a weighted form of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic. Its significance comes from permutation, and its scores are normalised for set size.
Permuting samples gives a self-contained test that respects the correlation between genes; permuting genes gives a competitive test that assumes independence and can produce discoveries from co-regulation alone.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis
text:
Reading
ISLR does not cover gene set analysis; its Chapter 13 on multiple testing is the background for the correction step. The original GSEA paper (Subramanian et al. 2005) is readable and explains the motivation, the running sum and the normalisation. Goeman and Bühlmann (2007) discusses the difference between competitive and self-contained tests and the role of correlation between genes.

title: Appendix A — Linear models: a worked reference
text:
Where this chapter fits {#sec-fit}
This appendix is a reference, not a lecture. The recurring idea of this course is that statistics arises when a simple model approximates a complex data-generating process. The response is split into a deterministic component and a residual drawn from an assumed distribution, and the degrees of freedom control how sharply the data can resolve that split. Day 1 introduced these ideas; this appendix works through the full lm workflow for readers who want to see it in detail.
The linear model (lm) is the reference realisation of that idea. It makes one especially convenient assumption about the residual: it is Gaussian, with a single constant variance \(\sigma^2\) that is the same for every observation. Regression, ANOVA, ANCOVA and factorial ANOVA are all the same linear model with different predictors; the workflow to fit and interpret them is identical.
This chapter walks through that workflow twice, in full, so that it becomes a reusable template:
For each, the same seven steps are followed: inspect and visualise the data, fit the maximal model, run the diagnostics, select among nested models, read the statistics tables, perform the post-hoc analysis with emmeans, and interpret. The emphasis is on reading the output carefully — what each diagnostic plot and each table column actually reports.

title: Appendix A — Linear models: a worked reference
text:
KEY — Regression, ANOVA, ANCOVA and factorial ANOVA are not four different tools. They are one linear model with different mixes of continuous and categorical predictors. The workflow, learned once, transfers.


an ANCOVA — one continuous predictor (a nutrient gradient) and one categorical predictor (light regime), and
a factorial ANOVA — two categorical predictors (nutrient level and grazing pressure) with an interaction.

title: Appendix A — Linear models: a worked reference
section: Data types and the model formula
text:
Data types and the model formula
Which linear model is being run is decided entirely by the types of the predictors:



Predictors
Common name
R formula




one continuous
simple regression
y ~ x


several continuous
multiple regression
y ~ x1 + x2


one categorical
one-way ANOVA
y ~ A


two+ categorical
factorial ANOVA
y ~ A * B


continuous + categorical
ANCOVA
y ~ x + A





DEF — In an R formula, A * B expands to A + B + A:B: the two main effects plus their interaction A:B. Writing A + B fits an additive model that constrains the interaction to zero.
The response is always continuous here. The residual assumption — Gaussian, constant variance, independent, no outliers — is what makes it a linear model, and it is the first thing the diagnostics check.

title: Appendix A — Linear models: a worked reference
section: Reading model shapes: a visual gallery
text:
Reading model shapes: a visual gallery
Before fitting anything, it is useful to know what the possible answers look like. The plots in this section carry no data; they are drawn directly from chosen coefficients, purely to train the eye. When a real fitted model is later examined, its picture is matched against these canonical shapes to read off which terms matter.

ANCOVA shapes
An ANCOVA fits a line for each level of the factor. Only two things can differ between those lines: their height (the factor or intercept effect) and their slope (the factor × covariate interaction). That gives four canonical outcomes.


Code
library(ggplot2)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 50)

anc_line <- function(int_s, slope_s, int_off, slope_off, panel) {
  rbind(
    data.frame(x, y = int_s + slope_s * x,
               group = "shade", panel = panel),
    data.frame(x, y = (int_s + int_off) + (slope_s + slope_off) * x,
               group = "sun",   panel = panel)
  )
}

anc_gallery <- rbind(
  anc_line(2, 0.30, 1.5, 0.35, "Interaction: slopes differ"),
  anc_line(2, 0.30, 1.5, 0.00, "Main effects only: parallel, offset"),
  anc_line(2, 0.30, 0.0, 0.00, "No factor effect: lines coincide"),
  anc_line(2, 0.00, 1.5, 0.00, "No covariate effect: flat, offset")
)
anc_gallery$panel <- factor(anc_gallery$panel,
                            levels = unique(anc_gallery$panel))

ggplot(anc_gallery, aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = "Covariate (e.g. nutrient)", y = "Response", colour = "Factor") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")





Four canonical ANCOVA outcomes, drawn from fixed coefficients (no data). Top-left: slopes differ (interaction). Top-right: parallel lines offset by the factor (main effects, no interaction). Bottom-left: lines coincide (no factor effect). Bottom-right: flat lines offset by the factor (no covariate effect).




The four panels exhaust the possibilities for two lines. In the top-left panel the lines diverge: the covariate effect depends on the group, and the interaction term is required. In the top-right panel the lines are parallel but offset: both main effects are present, the interaction is absent. In the bottom-left panel the lines coincide, so the factor has no effect; in the bottom-right panel the lines are flat, so the covariate has none.


KEY — In an ANCOVA, two questions are posed to the picture in order. Different slopes? → retain the interaction; the covariate effect depends on the group. Same slope but different height? → drop the interaction, retain both main effects. Same line? → the factor has no effect. Flat? → the covariate has no effect.

⚠ When the interaction is present (top-left), the covariate cannot be summarised by a single slope, nor the factor by a single gap — each depends on the other. Only the parallel case (top-right) admits a “one slope, one offset” description.



Factorial ANOVA shapes
A factorial design has no covariate — only cell means — so the natural picture is the interaction plot: cell means joined across one factor, one line per level of the other. Parallel lines mean the factors act additively; non-parallel lines mean they interact.


Code
fac_cells <- function(cells, panel) {
  g <- expand.grid(FactorB = c("none", "low", "high"),
                   FactorA = c("A: low", "A: high"))
  g$FactorB <- factor(g$FactorB, levels = c("none", "low", "high"))
  g$mean    <- cells
  g$panel   <- panel
  g
}

fac_gallery <- rbind(
  fac_cells(c(5, 5, 5,  5, 5, 5), "No effects"),
  fac_cells(c(4, 4, 4,  7, 7, 7), "One main effect (A)"),
  fac_cells(c(6, 5, 4,  9, 8, 7), "Two main effects (additive)"),
  fac_cells(c(6, 5, 4,  9, 7, 2), "Interaction (non-parallel)")
)
fac_gallery$panel <- factor(fac_gallery$panel,
                            levels = unique(fac_gallery$panel))

ggplot(fac_gallery, aes(FactorB, mean, colour = FactorA, group = FactorA)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = "Factor B", y = "Mean response", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")





Four canonical factorial outcomes as interaction plots (no data). Parallel lines (top row and bottom-left) indicate additive effects; only the bottom-right panel, with non-parallel lines, shows an interaction.




In the first three panels the two lines are parallel: the vertical gap between the levels of A is the same at every level of B, so the effects are additive and each can be described separately. Only the bottom-right panel shows non-parallel lines, the signature of an interaction.


KEY — The single most useful habit in factorial ANOVA is to look for parallelism. Parallel lines → additive main effects, interpretable separately. Non-parallel → an interaction, and the main effects can no longer be read on their own. Everything in the worked factorial case below returns to this one visual check.

DEF — Additive (top-right): the vertical gap between the two A lines is the same at every level of B; the effect of A does not depend on B. Interaction (bottom-right): that gap changes across B.

With these shapes in mind, two simulated cases are fitted and their output matched back to this gallery.

title: Appendix A — Linear models: a worked reference
section: Case 1 — ANCOVA: a gradient and a grouping
text:
Case 1 — ANCOVA: a gradient and a grouping

The question and the data
Leaf nitrogen content (%) is measured on plants along a soil nutrient gradient, in two light regimes (sun versus shade). Three biological questions arise:

Does leaf nitrogen rise with soil nutrients (a slope question)?
Does light regime shift leaf nitrogen up or down (an intercept question)?
And — the question that decides the model — does the nutrient slope itself differ between sun and shade (an interaction question)?


set.seed(42)
n        <- 160
nutrient <- runif(n, 0, 10)                       # soil nutrient index
light    <- factor(sample(c("shade", "sun"), n, replace = TRUE),
                   levels = c("shade", "sun"))     # shade = reference level

# True process: parallel lines. Sun raises the intercept by ~0.9; the slope
# (0.35 % nitrogen per nutrient unit) is the SAME in both light regimes.

Slope <- 0.35
Intercept <- (1.2 + 0.9 * (light == "sun"))
mu     <- Intercept + Slope * nutrient
leaf_N <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = 0.9)           # constant SD => homoscedastic
datA   <- data.frame(leaf_N, nutrient, light, Intercept)
head(datA)

#>     leaf_N nutrient light Intercept
#> 1 4.243848 9.148060 shade       1.2
#> 2 4.415160 9.370754   sun       2.1
#> 3 3.248375 2.861395   sun       2.1
#> 4 3.780102 8.304476 shade       1.2
#> 5 4.877122 6.417455   sun       2.1
#> 6 5.206016 5.190959   sun       2.1


The first rows show the four columns of the simulated data frame: the response leaf_N, the covariate nutrient, the factor light, and the true intercept for each observation, retained for reference. The data were generated with parallel lines and a constant residual standard deviation of 0.9; the analysis below should recover both facts.


⚠ The reference level of every factor must be checked, since every categorical coefficient is a contrast against it. Here shade is the reference, so lightsun denotes “sun relative to shade”. It is set deliberately with factor(..., levels = ) or relevel().


Numeric and visual summary

summary(datA[,1:3])

#>      leaf_N          nutrient          light   
#>  Min.   :0.1155   Min.   :0.002389   shade:77  
#>  1st Qu.:2.5723   1st Qu.:2.824263   sun  :83  
#>  Median :3.6073   Median :5.766484             
#>  Mean   :3.5258   Mean   :5.333326             
#>  3rd Qu.:4.4215   3rd Qu.:7.673367             
#>  Max.   :7.3610   Max.   :9.888917


The response ranges over roughly one order of magnitude, the nutrient index spans its full 0–10 range, and the two light groups are close to balanced. The data are plotted before modelling, because the picture indicates what model to expect.

ggplot(datA, aes(nutrient, leaf_N, colour = light)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Soil nutrient index", y = "Leaf nitrogen (%)", colour = "Light")




Leaf nitrogen against the nutrient gradient, coloured by light regime. The two fitted lines appear close to parallel — a visual indication that the interaction is unnecessary.




The two lines are offset — sun above shade — but close to parallel. Matched against the gallery, this is the top-right panel: a light effect on the intercept and a negligible interaction are expected.


KEY — In an ANCOVA plot, two questions are visible directly: do the lines have different heights (a light effect) and different slopes (an interaction)? Here the lines are offset but close to parallel.


Fitting the maximal model
The analysis starts with the most complex model the design justifies — here, one that allows the slopes to differ — and simplifies downward from it.

mA_full <- lm(leaf_N ~ light + nutrient + light:nutrient , data = datA)   # light*nutrient as shorthand



DEF — Maximal model: the largest model justified by the design, fitted first. Model selection then removes terms that do not earn their degrees of freedom in explanatory power, yielding a minimal adequate model.


Model diagnostics
The linear model rests on the residual being Gaussian with constant variance, and on no single point dominating the fit. All three conditions are checked.

Homoscedasticity

residualPlots(mA_full, tests = FALSE, layout = c(1, 3))




Residuals against each predictor and against the fitted values. A flat, patternless band supports constant variance.






KEY — Residual plots are read for two features: a trend in the mean (the fitted curve departing from horizontal → the mean structure is wrong, e.g. a missing quadratic term) and a change in spread (a funnel → heteroscedasticity). Neither should be present.
The first panel, against light, shows homogeneity of variance: the two boxplots have the same height and their medians sit close to zero. The second panel, against nutrient, shows a blue curve (a quadratic fit) deviating slightly from the dashed straight line; the deviation is small relative to the spread of the residuals, and the spread itself remains even along the gradient — again homoscedastic. The third panel, against the fitted values, combines the first two and carries the same interpretation as the nutrient panel.
The absence of a spread trend can be confirmed numerically through the correlation between the absolute residuals and the fitted values.

cor(abs(resid(mA_full)), fitted(mA_full))

#> [1] 0.02235455


The correlation is essentially zero: the magnitude of the residuals does not change with the fitted value, which is the numerical statement of constant variance.


Normality of residuals

qqPlot(residuals(mA_full), id = list(n=4))




QQ-plot of studentized residuals against the reference distribution (car::qqPlot). Points on the line indicate approximate normality; the dashed envelope is a pointwise confidence band. Note that residuals(Model_name) must be passed to obtain the residuals; the id argument labels the row numbers of the most extreme observations.




#> [1] 109 127  44 129


The points track the diagonal and remain within the envelope, with no heavy tails or systematic curvature. The four labelled points are merely the most extreme residuals and lie inside the band. A formal test is applied as support.

shapiro.test(resid(mA_full))

#> 
#>  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
#> 
#> data:  resid(mA_full)
#> W = 0.99459, p-value = 0.8229


The Shapiro–Wilk statistic is \(W = 0.995\) with \(p = 0.82\): there is no evidence against normality.


⚠ A non-significant Shapiro–Wilk test does not prove normality; it means no evidence against it was found. With small samples the test has little power; with very large samples it flags biologically trivial departures. The QQ-plot is primary and the test is support.


Influential observations

influenceIndexPlot(mA_full, vars = c("Cook", "Studentized", "hat"))




Influence diagnostics: Cook’s distance, studentized residuals (with Bonferroni outlier p-values), and hat-values (leverage).






DEF — Leverage (hat-value) measures how unusual a point is in the predictor space; Cook’s distance combines leverage and residual size to measure how much a point actually moves the fit. A point can have high leverage yet low influence if it lies on the trend.
No Cook’s distance approaches the usual thresholds of concern (all are well below 0.5, let alone 1) in the first panel, and no studentized residual is a Bonferroni outlier in the second. The third panel shows the leverage values, none of which stands apart from the rest. The outlierTest formalises the second panel.

outlierTest(mA_full)

#> No Studentized residuals with Bonferroni p < 0.05
#> Largest |rstudent|:
#>     rstudent unadjusted p-value Bonferroni p
#> 109 -2.82079          0.0054176      0.86682


The largest studentized residual has a Bonferroni-adjusted \(p > 0.05\), so there is no evidence for any outlier.
A rule of thumb exists for flagging unusually high leverage, analogous to that for Cook’s distance: a hat value greater than 2.5 times the mean hat value.

h    <- hatvalues(mA_full)
cutoff <- 2.5 * mean(h)          # cutoff for leverage value
which(h > cutoff)                # indices of high-leverage points

#> named integer(0)


The output named integer(0) indicates that no observation exceeds the cut-off, which is the desired result.


Integration: the diagnostic verdict
The three diagnostic families agree. The residual plots and the near-zero correlation between absolute residuals and fitted values establish constant variance; the QQ-plot and the Shapiro–Wilk test establish approximate normality; the influence plot, the outlier test and the leverage cut-off establish that no single observation drives the fit. All three assumptions of the linear model therefore hold for the maximal model, and model selection and interpretation may proceed on it.



Model selection
Is the interaction needed? The maximal model is compared with the additive model that constrains the slopes to be parallel. Because the models are nested, a partial \(F\)-test is exact.

mA_add <- lm(leaf_N ~ light + nutrient, data = datA)
anova(mA_add, mA_full)   # H0: interaction coefficient = 0

#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: leaf_N ~ light + nutrient
#> Model 2: leaf_N ~ light + nutrient + light:nutrient
#>   Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
#> 1    157 114.33                           
#> 2    156 114.31  1    0.0247 0.0337 0.8546




KEY — anova(small, big) on two nested lm objects is a partial \(F\)-test: it asks whether the extra term in the larger model explains significantly more variance than its extra degrees of freedom would by chance. A large \(p\) means “the simpler model is adequate”.
The interaction adds essentially nothing (\(F_{1,156} = 0.03\), \(p = 0.85\)): the extra term reduces the residual sum of squares by only 0.02. It is dropped, as the near-parallel lines in the plot anticipated. AIC provides a second, non-nested criterion.

AIC(mA_full, mA_add,
    lm(leaf_N ~ nutrient, data = datA),
    lm(leaf_N ~ light,    data = datA))

#>                                    df      AIC
#> mA_full                             5 410.2585
#> mA_add                              4 408.2931
#> lm(leaf_N ~ nutrient, data = datA)  3 434.8135
#> lm(leaf_N ~ light, data = datA)     3 546.7514




DEF — \(\mathrm{AIC} = 2k - 2\ln\hat{L}\), with \(k\) the number of parameters and \(\hat L\) the maximised likelihood. It rewards fit and penalises complexity, and unlike the \(F\)-test it can compare non-nested models. A difference of \(\gtrsim 2\) is usually taken as meaningful. Day 5 returns to this.
The additive model has the lowest AIC (408.3 against 410.3 for the interaction model): dropping the interaction improved the penalised fit. Both models far outperform either predictor alone. The additive model is therefore the minimal adequate model, and the \(F\)-test and AIC agree on this conclusion.


Reading the statistics table

summary(mA_add)

#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = leaf_N ~ light + nutrient, data = datA)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -2.34871 -0.62571  0.02705  0.52758  2.16964 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  1.30890    0.15860   8.253 5.92e-14 ***
#> lightsun     0.74771    0.13509   5.535 1.28e-07 ***
#> nutrient     0.34294    0.02308  14.856  < 2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 0.8534 on 157 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.6109, Adjusted R-squared:  0.6059 
#> F-statistic: 123.2 on 2 and 157 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


This table is the core of the analysis and is read column by column.


KEY — Every coefficient is interpreted holding the other predictors fixed. nutrient is the slope within a light level; lightsun is the gap between light levels at the same nutrient value. That is the purpose of placing them in one model.

(Intercept) = 1.31. The predicted leaf nitrogen for the reference combination: a shade plant at nutrient = 0. It anchors everything else.
lightsun = 0.748 (\(p = 1.3\times10^{-7}\)). At any given nutrient level, a sun plant has about 0.75 % more leaf nitrogen than a shade plant. The positive sign and small \(p\) confirm a clear light effect on the intercept.
nutrient = 0.343 (\(p < 2\times10^{-16}\)). For every one-unit rise in the soil nutrient index, leaf nitrogen rises by about 0.34 %, in both light regimes (the slope is shared because the interaction was dropped). This is the gradient effect, and it is strong.
Std. Error, t value, Pr(>|t|). Each \(t\) is the estimate divided by its standard error; the \(p\)-value tests whether that coefficient differs from zero. Small SEs relative to the estimates give large \(t\) values and small \(p\)-values.
Residual standard error = 0.853 on 157 df. The typical size of a residual, the estimate of \(\sigma\) (close to the 0.9 used in the simulation). Despite R’s label this is a standard deviation of residuals, not a sampling standard error. The 157 df are \(n - 3\): 160 observations minus three estimated parameters (two light-level means and one nutrient slope).
Multiple \(R^2\) = 0.611. The model explains about 61 % of the variance in leaf nitrogen. Adjusted \(R^2\) = 0.606 applies a small-sample penalty and is the appropriate figure to report.
\(F\)-statistic = 123 on 2 and 157 df (\(p < 2.2\times10^{-16}\)). The omnibus test: the model as a whole explains far more than nothing.

The anova() table presents the same fit from the variance-partition side — how the total sum of squares splits across terms.

anova(mA_add)

#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Response: leaf_N
#>            Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> light       1  18.771  18.771  25.775 1.074e-06 ***
#> nutrient    1 160.727 160.727 220.704 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> Residuals 157 114.335   0.728                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




⚠ anova() on one model gives sequential (Type-I) sums of squares — each term is added in order, adjusting only for the terms above it. For an additive model with near-orthogonal predictors this is unproblematic, but with correlated predictors the order matters. For unbalanced or interaction models, marginal (Type-II/III) tests such as car::Anova() are preferred.
Nutrient enters first and captures the largest sum of squares (157.2); light adds a further significant portion (22.3, \(p = 1.3\times10^{-7}\)), matching its coefficient test. The residual mean square, 0.728, is the estimate of \(\sigma^2\), the square of the residual standard error above.


Post-hoc analysis with emmeans
The coefficient table already answers the questions, but emmeans places the answers on the response scale as estimated marginal means — model-based predictions at representative predictor values — which are easier to report and to plot, and which generalise to more complex designs.


DEF — Estimated marginal mean (EMM): the model’s predicted mean for a group, with any continuous covariate held at its average value (here nutrient at its mean, ≈ 5.3). It is the “all else equal” group mean.

# Estimated marginal means for the two light regimes, at the mean nutrient level
emm_light <- emmeans(mA_add, ~ light)
emm_light

#>  light emmean     SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
#>  shade   3.14 0.0973 157     2.95     3.33
#>  sun     3.89 0.0937 157     3.70     4.07
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95


The two EMMs are about 3.14 % for shade and 3.89 % for sun, each at the average nutrient level, with their standard errors and confidence intervals. These are the group means the model predicts once the covariate has been held constant.

# Pairwise contrast between the light regimes
pairs(emm_light)

#>  contrast    estimate    SE  df t.ratio p.value
#>  shade - sun   -0.748 0.135 157  -5.535  <.0001


The contrast is 0.75 % — identical, as it must be, to the lightsun coefficient, because in an additive model the light gap is the same at every nutrient value. It is highly significant (\(t = 5.5\), \(p \approx 1.3\times10^{-7}\)).
For the continuous predictor, the analogous tool is emtrends, which reports the slope and can compare slopes across groups.

emtrends(mA_add, ~ light, var = "nutrient")

#>  light nutrient.trend     SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
#>  shade          0.343 0.0231 157    0.297    0.389
#>  sun            0.343 0.0231 157    0.297    0.389
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95


The two nutrient slopes are 0.343 in each light regime, with identical confidence intervals.


KEY — In the additive model the two nutrient slopes are equal by construction, so their confidence intervals coincide. This is exactly the parallel-lines assumption that was tested and accepted. Had the interaction been retained, emtrends would show two different slopes and allow a test of their difference.


Interpretation and final plot
Taken together: leaf nitrogen rises with soil nutrients at about 0.34 % per unit, identically in sun and shade, and sun plants sit about 0.75 % higher than shade plants at every point along the gradient. There is no evidence that light changes the slope of the relationship, only its height. These are the parameters that were simulated (slope 0.35, offset 0.9, \(\sigma\) 0.9), recovered within their standard errors.

ggplot(datA, aes(nutrient, leaf_N, colour = light)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict(mA_add)), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Soil nutrient index", y = "Leaf nitrogen (%)", colour = "Light")




Final additive ANCOVA model: parallel regression lines separated by a constant light effect.




The fitted lines are exactly parallel, since the model contains no interaction; the vertical distance between them is the lightsun coefficient.

title: Appendix A — Linear models: a worked reference
section: Case 2 — Factorial ANOVA: two factors and an interaction
text:
Case 2 — Factorial ANOVA: two factors and an interaction

The question and the data
The second case has two categorical predictors. Algae are grown and their biomass (mg) measured under two crossed treatments: nutrient level (low, high) and grazing pressure (none, low, high) — a \(2 \times 3\) factorial design with 12 replicates per cell. The biological expectation is an interaction: grazers suppress algal biomass, but the suppression should be much stronger when nutrients are high and there is more algae to consume.

set.seed(7)
design <- expand.grid(rep      = 1:12,
                      nutrient = c("low", "high"),
                      grazer   = c("none", "low", "high"))
design$nutrient <- factor(design$nutrient, levels = c("low", "high"))
design$grazer   <- factor(design$grazer,   levels = c("none", "low", "high"))

# True cell means with an interaction: at LOW nutrient grazers barely matter;
# at HIGH nutrient grazers cut biomass sharply.
cell_mean <- function(nut, grz) {
  base  <- 5
  n_eff <- ifelse(nut == "high", 8, 0)
  g_eff <- c(none = 0, low = -1, high = -2)[as.character(grz)]
  i_eff <- ifelse(nut == "high",
                  c(none = 0, low = -3, high = -6)[as.character(grz)], 0)
  base + n_eff + g_eff + i_eff
}
mu      <- mapply(cell_mean, design$nutrient, design$grazer)
biomass <- rnorm(nrow(design), mean = mu, sd = 1.6)
datF    <- data.frame(biomass, nutrient = design$nutrient, grazer = design$grazer)



DEF — A factorial design crosses every level of one factor with every level of another. Balanced means equal replication in every cell (here 12), which makes the sums of squares independent and the interpretation cleanest.


Visualising the design
For factorial data the key picture is the interaction plot: group means joined across one factor, one line per level of the other. Non-parallel lines signal an interaction.

ggplot(datF, aes(grazer, biomass, colour = nutrient, group = nutrient)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.1) +
  labs(x = "Grazing pressure", y = "Algal biomass (mg)", colour = "Nutrient")




Interaction plot. Grazing barely lowers biomass at low nutrients but sharply lowers it at high nutrients — the lines are far from parallel, the visual signature of an interaction.




The high-nutrient line falls steeply across the grazing levels while the low-nutrient line is nearly flat. Matched against the factorial gallery, this is the bottom-right panel: a significant nutrient:grazer term is expected.


KEY — Parallel lines → the two factors act additively (their effects sum). Converging, diverging or crossing lines → an interaction: the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.


Fit and diagnostics

mF_full <- lm(biomass ~ nutrient * grazer, data = datF)

The diagnostics are read in the same way as for the ANCOVA.

residualPlots(mF_full, tests = FALSE, layout = c(1, 3))




Residuals against fitted values for the factorial model. With categorical predictors the residuals cluster at the six fitted cell means; the check is that the spread is similar across clusters.




The residuals form vertical stripes, one per cell, of comparable height: the spread is similar across the six cells, so the constant-variance assumption is supported.


⚠ With only categorical predictors the residual-versus-fitted plot shows vertical stripes, one per cell; this is expected, not a defect. The check is that the stripes have similar height (equal spread across cells, i.e. homoscedasticity), not that they form a cloud.

qqPlot(residuals(mF_full), id = list(n = 6))




Normal QQ-plot of the factorial-model residuals.




#> [1] 12  1 24 10 13 57


The QQ-plot is straight and all points, including the six labelled extremes, lie within the envelope.

shapiro.test(resid(mF_full))

#> 
#>  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
#> 
#> data:  resid(mF_full)
#> W = 0.98757, p-value = 0.703


Shapiro–Wilk is comfortably non-significant (\(W = 0.99\), \(p = 0.70\)), agreeing with the QQ-plot.


Integration: the diagnostic verdict
The stripes in the residual plot are of comparable height, the QQ-plot is straight, and the formal test finds no evidence against normality. The equal replication (12 per cell) also means that the sum-of-squares subtleties of unbalanced designs do not arise. The assumptions hold, and the ANOVA table can be interpreted.


The ANOVA table and model selection
For a factorial model the anova() table is the primary result: it partitions the variance among the two main effects and their interaction.

anova(mF_full)

#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Response: biomass
#>                 Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
#> nutrient         1 499.68  499.68 218.665 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> grazer           2 321.40  160.70  70.323 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> nutrient:grazer  2  98.79   49.40  21.617 6.015e-08 ***
#> Residuals       66 150.82    2.29                      
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




KEY — A factorial ANOVA table is read from the bottom up. If the interaction is significant, the main-effect rows above it are not directly interpretable on their own; the effect of each factor must be described within levels of the other (the simple effects), because by definition each depends on the other.
Every row is significant, but the one that governs interpretation is the interaction: nutrient:grazer, \(F_{2,66} = 21.6\), \(p = 6.0\times10^{-8}\). Because it is significant, the full model is retained — the reverse of the ANCOVA decision. The nested test confirms that the interaction earns its two degrees of freedom.

mF_add <- lm(biomass ~ nutrient + grazer, data = datF)
anova(mF_add, mF_full)

#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: biomass ~ nutrient + grazer
#> Model 2: biomass ~ nutrient * grazer
#>   Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
#> 1     68 249.61                                  
#> 2     66 150.82  2    98.794 21.617 6.015e-08 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Dropping the interaction costs 98.8 in residual sum of squares for two degrees of freedom (\(p = 6\times10^{-8}\)). AIC is examined for confirmation.

AIC(mF_full, mF_add)

#>         df      AIC
#> mF_full  7 271.5650
#> mF_add   5 303.8408


Removing the interaction raises AIC by 32 (272 → 304). Both criteria agree: the interaction stays.
The coefficient table presents the same result in contrast form.

summary(mF_full)

#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = biomass ~ nutrient * grazer, data = datF)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#> -3.0494 -0.7608 -0.0445  0.8981  3.7983 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                         Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)               5.5485     0.4364  12.715  < 2e-16 ***
#> nutrienthigh              8.2801     0.6171  13.417  < 2e-16 ***
#> grazerlow                -1.4899     0.6171  -2.414 0.018552 *  
#> grazerhigh               -2.2742     0.6171  -3.685 0.000463 ***
#> nutrienthigh:grazerlow   -3.3205     0.8728  -3.805 0.000313 ***
#> nutrienthigh:grazerhigh  -5.7135     0.8728  -6.547 1.03e-08 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 1.512 on 66 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.8591, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8485 
#> F-statistic: 80.51 on 5 and 66 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16




⚠ In a model with an interaction, grazerlow = −1.49 is not “the effect of low grazing”. It is that effect only at the reference nutrient level (low). The nutrienthigh:grazerlow term (−3.32) states that the grazing effect is a further 3.3 mg more negative when nutrients are high. Main-effect coefficients in an interaction model are always “the effect at the other factor’s reference level”.
Reading the interaction coefficients directly: nutrienthigh:grazerhigh = −5.71 (\(p = 10^{-8}\)) means that moving from no grazing to high grazing costs 5.7 mg more under high nutrients than under low nutrients. The model explains 86 % of the variance (adjusted \(R^2 = 0.85\)). Coefficients relative to a shifting reference are, however, awkward to report — which is exactly what emmeans resolves.


Post-hoc analysis with emmeans: simple effects and contrasts
With a significant interaction, the appropriate post-hoc question is not “what is the overall grazing effect?” but “what is the grazing effect within each nutrient level?” — the simple effects. emmeans expresses this with the | (“by”) operator.

# Estimated marginal mean biomass for every cell of the design
emm_cells <- emmeans(mF_full, ~ grazer | nutrient)
emm_cells

#> nutrient = low:
#>  grazer emmean    SE df lower.CL upper.CL
#>  none     5.55 0.436 66     4.68     6.42
#>  low      4.06 0.436 66     3.19     4.93
#>  high     3.27 0.436 66     2.40     4.15
#> 
#> nutrient = high:
#>  grazer emmean    SE df lower.CL upper.CL
#>  none    13.83 0.436 66    12.96    14.70
#>  low      9.02 0.436 66     8.15     9.89
#>  high     5.84 0.436 66     4.97     6.71
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95


The output lists six cell means, grouped by nutrient level, with their standard errors and confidence intervals. Within the low-nutrient group the three means are close together; within the high-nutrient group they fall sharply with grazing.


KEY — ~ grazer | nutrient reads as “grazer means, separately within each nutrient level”. This is the natural way to unpack an interaction: six cell means, grouped so that grazing is compared within low- and within high-nutrient conditions.
The pairwise grazing contrasts are computed within each nutrient level and FDR-adjusted for multiple comparisons.

pairs(emm_cells, adjust = "fdr")

#> nutrient = low:
#>  contrast    estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  none - low     1.490 0.617 66   2.414  0.0278
#>  none - high    2.274 0.617 66   3.685  0.0014
#>  low - high     0.784 0.617 66   1.271  0.2082
#> 
#> nutrient = high:
#>  contrast    estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  none - low     4.810 0.617 66   7.795  <.0001
#>  none - high    7.988 0.617 66  12.943  <.0001
#>  low - high     3.177 0.617 66   5.149  <.0001
#> 
#> P value adjustment: fdr method for 3 tests




DEF — Simple effect: the effect of one factor at a fixed level of another. A significant interaction means the simple effects differ across levels — here, the grazing contrasts are small at low nutrients and large at high nutrients.
The contrast that captures the biology is none versus high grazing: about 2.3 mg at low nutrients but about 8.0 mg at high nutrients. Grazing barely reduces biomass when there is little algae to begin with, but removes a large fraction when nutrients drive high production — the interaction, now stated as two concrete, reportable numbers rather than as a coefficient against a moving reference.
The design can equally be sliced the other way — the nutrient effect within each grazing level.

# Nutrient effect within each grazing level
pairs(emmeans(mF_full, ~ nutrient | grazer), adjust = "fdr")

#> grazer = none:
#>  contrast   estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  low - high    -8.28 0.617 66 -13.417  <.0001
#> 
#> grazer = low:
#>  contrast   estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  low - high    -4.96 0.617 66  -8.036  <.0001
#> 
#> grazer = high:
#>  contrast   estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  low - high    -2.57 0.617 66  -4.159  0.0001


The nutrient effect is large under no grazing and diminishes as grazing intensifies; it is the same interaction viewed from the other factor. emmeans would also provide marginal main effects averaged over the other factor, but with a strong interaction such averages can mislead.


⚠ emmeans will report main-effect means averaged over the other factor even when the interaction is significant. Those marginal means average over a relationship that changes; they should be reported only with the interaction explicitly described alongside, or they impose a single number on two different stories.


Interpretation
The two factors do not act independently. High nutrients raise algal biomass substantially; grazing lowers it; but the size of the grazing effect depends on nutrient level — it is minor under low nutrients and large under high nutrients. The correct summary is the set of simple effects, not a single “grazing effect”, because no single grazing effect exists to report.

ggplot(datF, aes(grazer, biomass, fill = nutrient)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "col", position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar",
               position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Grazing pressure", y = "Algal biomass (mg)", fill = "Nutrient")




Cell means with standard errors. The widening gap between nutrient levels as grazing increases is the interaction made visible.




The bars show the six cell means; the gap between the nutrient levels narrows from left to right, which is the interaction in its final, reportable form.

title: Appendix A — Linear models: a worked reference
text:
Summary and bridge
Both analyses used one workflow: inspect and plot, fit the maximal model, check the residual assumptions, select among nested models, read the tables, and interpret through emmeans. The two cases differed in one decision — whether the interaction survived model selection:

The ANCOVA dropped its interaction (\(p = 0.85\)): parallel lines, a single shared nutrient slope, and a constant light offset. Interpretation consists of the two main-effect coefficients directly.
The factorial ANOVA retained its interaction (\(p = 6\times10^{-8}\)): the grazing effect depends on nutrient level, so interpretation consists of the simple effects within each level, not a single main effect.



KEY — The whole of “which model?” reduces to: fit the maximal model, then ask whether each term earns its degrees of freedom. The interaction test is not a formality; it decides whether main effects or simple effects are reported.
Everything here rested on the residual being Gaussian with constant variance. That pair of assumptions is convenient, and for these two data sets it held. But much biological data violates it: counts are skewed and bounded at zero, proportions are bounded in \([0,1]\), and variance very often grows with the mean. Day 6 shows how a model can use another distribution, through maximum likelihood, with logistic regression as the main example.
crumbs: A  Linear models: a worked reference

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
text:
Data are points
You have met linear algebra before, as rules for computing with vectors and matrices. This appendix is about something else: what those rules look like, and why a statistician needs them. Every method in this course turns out to be a question about geometry. Which sample is nearest? How far is a measurement from a model? In which direction does a data cloud vary most? How can a coefficient be made smaller?
It builds that geometry from pictures, using a small set of objects that return throughout:
\[
\mathbf{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{M}^\top\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} .
\]
Each section ends with a question to check your understanding, with the answer folded away. The formal definitions, the proofs and the algorithms behind the pictures are in Appendix C.
A tumour sample measured on two genes is a pair of numbers, and a pair of numbers is a point in the plane, or equivalently an arrow from the origin to that point. Forty samples measured on two genes are forty points: a data cloud.
Code
set.seed(11)
cloud <- MASS::mvrnorm(40, mu = c(6, 5), Sigma = matrix(c(1.5, 1, 1, 1.2), 2))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plane(c(0, 9), c(0, 8), main = "one sample", xlab = "gene 1 (log expression)",
      ylab = "gene 2 (log expression)")
arrow(c(0, 0), cloud[1, ], col = col_blue)
points(cloud[1, 1], cloud[1, 2], pch = 19, col = col_blue, cex = 1.3)
text(cloud[1, 1], cloud[1, 2], sprintf("(%.1f, %.1f)", cloud[1, 1], cloud[1, 2]), pos = 4)
plane(c(0, 9), c(0, 8), main = "forty samples", xlab = "gene 1 (log expression)",
      ylab = "gene 2 (log expression)")
points(cloud, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor(col_blue, 0.7))








Figure B.1: Left: one sample, measured on two genes, is a point and also an arrow from the origin. Right: forty samples form a data cloud. With 20,000 genes each sample is a point in a space of 20,000 dimensions, which cannot be drawn but obeys the same geometry.
In a data matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) each row is one sample and each column one variable, so an \(n \times p\) matrix is a cloud of \(n\) points in \(p\) dimensions. Everything in this appendix can be drawn for \(p = 2\), and everything remains true for \(p = 20{,}000\).

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
text:
⚠ Expression data are usually stored with genes as rows and samples as columns. Statistical functions such as lm, prcomp and glmnet expect samples as rows. Check dim(X) before anything else, and transpose with t(X) if needed.






CautionCheck yourself



An expression file has 20,000 rows and 48 columns, one column per patient. You want to compare patients. How many points are in the cloud, and in how many dimensions do they live? What must you do before calling prcomp()?






TipAnswer





There are 48 points, one per patient, in a space of 20,000 dimensions, one per gene. prcomp() treats rows as observations, so the matrix must first be transposed with t() to give 48 rows and 20,000 columns.
