title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
section: Length and distance: two ways to measure
text:
Length and distance: two ways to measure
How long is the arrow \(\mathbf{b} = (1, 2)\)? The answer depends on how you are allowed to travel. As the crow flies, Pythagoras gives the Euclidean or L2 norm. Along the grid, like a taxi in Manhattan, you add the steps in each direction, which gives the Manhattan or L1 norm:
\[
\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 = \sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_p^2},
\qquad
\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_1 = |x_1| + |x_2| + \dots + |x_p| .
\]
For \(\mathbf{b}\) these are \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.24\) and \(3\). The distance between two points is the length of their difference, \(d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\rVert\).


DEF — A norm \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\) measures the length of a vector. The general family is the Lp norm, \(\big(\sum_j |x_j|^p\big)^{1/p}\), with \(p = 1\) and \(p = 2\) as the two important cases. Appendix C lists the three rules every norm must obey.
The clearest way to see the difference between the norms is to draw all vectors of length 1, the unit ball.


Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plane(c(-0.5, 2.5), c(-0.5, 2.5), main = "two routes to b = (1, 2)")
lines(c(0, 1, 1), c(0, 0, 2), col = col_orange, lwd = 3)
arrow(c(0, 0), b_vec, col = col_blue, lwd = 3)
text(0.5, 0, "1", pos = 1, col = col_orange); text(1, 1, "2", pos = 4, col = col_orange)
text(0.3, 1.1, expression(sqrt(5)), col = col_blue)

plane(c(-1.4, 1.4), c(-1.4, 1.4), main = "all vectors of length 1")
u <- unit_circle()
lines(u, col = col_blue, lwd = 2.5)
polygon(c(1, 0, -1, 0), c(0, 1, 0, -1), border = col_orange, lwd = 2.5)
polygon(c(1, -1, -1, 1), c(1, 1, -1, -1), border = col_grey, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("bottom", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.8, lwd = 2.5, lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       col = c(col_blue, col_orange, col_grey), legend = c(expression(L[2]), expression(L[1]), expression(L[infinity])))








Figure B.2: Left: the Euclidean norm measures the straight line (\(\sqrt 5\)), the Manhattan norm the route along the axes (\(1 + 2 = 3\)). Right: the vectors of length 1 form a circle for L2, a diamond for L1, and a square for the maximum norm L∞, which takes the largest coordinate.





The choice of norm is not neutral. Consider two cell samples, measured as log fold changes on two genes relative to a control at the origin: \(\mathbf{s}_1 = (3, 0)\) differs strongly in one gene, \(\mathbf{s}_2 = (2, 2)\) moderately in both.


Code
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plane(c(-3.5, 4.5), c(-3.4, 3.4), xlab = "gene 1 (log fold change)", ylab = "gene 2 (log fold change)")
polygon(c(3, 0, -3, 0), c(0, 3, 0, -3), border = col_orange, lwd = 2.5)
lines(3 * u, col = col_blue, lwd = 2.5)
points(c(0, 3, 2), c(0, 0, 2), pch = 19, cex = 1.2)
text(0, 0, "r", pos = 1); text(3, 0, expression(s[1]), pos = 4); text(2, 2, expression(s[2]), pos = 4)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, lwd = 2.5, col = c(col_blue, col_orange),
       legend = c("L2 distance 3", "L1 distance 3"))








Figure B.3: Both curves contain the points at distance 3 from the control r. Sample s₂ lies inside the circle, so it is closer than s₁ in the Euclidean norm, but outside the diamond, so it is further away than s₁ in the Manhattan norm.






s1 <- c(3, 0); s2 <- c(2, 2)
rbind(L2 = c(s1 = sqrt(sum(s1^2)), s2 = sqrt(sum(s2^2))),
      L1 = c(s1 = sum(abs(s1)),    s2 = sum(abs(s2))))

#>    s1       s2
#> L2  3 2.828427
#> L1  3 4.000000


In L2, \(\mathbf{s}_2\) is the nearest sample; in L1, \(\mathbf{s}_1\) is. Squaring makes the Euclidean norm sensitive to one large deviation (\(3^2 = 9 > 2^2 + 2^2 = 8\)), while the Manhattan norm adds deviations linearly.


KEY — “Nearest” depends on the norm. Choosing a distance is a modelling decision, with consequences for every method built on it.

↪ Clustering (Day 4) and KNN (Day 8) are built on distances, and both let you choose the norm.







CautionCheck yourself



Compute the L1 and L2 distance between \(\mathbf{a} = (3, 0)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (1, 2)\). Which norm gives the larger value, and is that always so?






TipAnswer





The difference is \(\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b} = (2, -2)\). Its L1 length is \(|2| + |-2| = 4\) and its L2 length is \(\sqrt{4 + 4} = \sqrt 8 \approx 2.83\). The L1 distance is never smaller than the L2 distance: the route along the axes is never shorter than the straight line. In the picture, the diamond lies inside the circle. The two are equal only when the difference has a single non-zero coordinate.

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
section: A preview: why the shape of the unit ball matters for regularisation
text:
A preview: why the shape of the unit ball matters for regularisation
The diamond and the circle return on Day 9 in a very different role. There, the coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\) of a regression are kept small by requiring that their norm stay within a budget \(s\):
\[
\text{minimise the residual sum of squares subject to } \lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2 \le s \;\text{(ridge)}\quad\text{or}\quad \lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1 \le s \;\text{(lasso)} .
\]
The residual sum of squares has elliptical contours around the least-squares estimate. The solution is the point where the smallest contour first touches the budget region.


Code
Q   <- matrix(c(1, 0.65, 0.65, 1), 2)          # shape of the RSS contours
b0  <- c(2.4, 1.0)                              # least-squares estimate
rss <- function(B) rowSums((B - matrix(b0, nrow(B), 2, byrow = TRUE)) %*% Q *
                           (B - matrix(b0, nrow(B), 2, byrow = TRUE)))
boundary <- function(kind, s, m = 20000) {
  if (kind == "L2") return(s * unit_circle(m))
  t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m / 4)
  rbind(cbind(s * (1 - t), s * t), cbind(-s * t, s * (1 - t)),
        cbind(-s * (1 - t), -s * t), cbind(s * t, -s * (1 - t)))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (kind in c("L1", "L2")) {
  s <- if (kind == "L1") 1.35 else 1.25
  B <- boundary(kind, s)
  hit <- B[which.min(rss(B)), ]
  plane(c(-1.5, 3.6), c(-1.5, 2.6), grid = FALSE,
        main = if (kind == "L1") "lasso: L1 budget" else "ridge: L2 budget",
        xlab = expression(beta[1]), ylab = expression(beta[2]))
  polygon(B, col = "#DCE6F1", border = col_blue)
  lev <- rss(matrix(hit, 1))
  for (f in c(0.35, 0.7, 1)) {
    e <- ellipse_A(Q, lev * f)
    lines(e[, 1] + b0[1], e[, 2] + b0[2], col = col_orange, lwd = 1.4)
  }
  points(b0[1], b0[2], pch = 19); text(b0[1], b0[2], "least squares", pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
  points(hit[1], hit[2], pch = 19, col = col_orange, cex = 1.3)
}








Figure B.4: Coefficient space for two coefficients. The ellipses are contours of the residual sum of squares around the least-squares estimate (black dot). The shaded region is the budget. Left: the L1 diamond has corners on the axes, and the first contact is at a corner, where β₂ is exactly zero. Right: the L2 circle has no corners, and the contact point has both coefficients non-zero.







KEY — The corners of the L1 diamond lie on the axes. That is why the lasso sets coefficients exactly to zero, and ridge regression does not.

↪ Day 9 develops this picture and the algebra behind it.







CautionCheck yourself



In the left panel, suppose the least-squares estimate moved straight upwards to \((2.4, 3)\). Would the lasso solution still have \(\beta_2 = 0\)? Think about which part of the diamond the ellipses would now reach first.






TipAnswer





Probably not. With the estimate high above the \(\beta_1\)-axis, the contours would first touch the diamond near its top corner or along its upper-right edge. On that edge both coefficients are non-zero, and at the top corner \(\beta_1\) is zero instead. Which coefficients the lasso sets to zero depends on where the least-squares estimate lies relative to the corners.

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
text:
The inner product: a shadow
The inner product (or dot product) of two vectors multiplies them coordinate by coordinate and adds:
\[
\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + \dots + a_pb_p .
\]
For our pair, \(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{b} = 3 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 2 = 3\). A single number, but it has a picture. Let light fall perpendicular to \(\mathbf{a}\): the shadow of \(\mathbf{b}\) on \(\mathbf{a}\) has length \(\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert\cos\theta\), and the inner product is that shadow times the length of \(\mathbf{a}\):
\[
\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{b} = \lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert\cos\theta .
\]


Code
par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1))
plane(c(-0.3, 3.5), c(-0.4, 2.4))
polygon(c(0, 1, 1, 0), c(0, 0, 2, 2), col = "grey95", border = NA)
segments(1, 0, 1, 2, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
lines(c(0, 1), c(0, 0), col = col_orange, lwd = 7)
arrow(c(0, 0), a_vec, col = "black"); arrow(c(0, 0), b_vec, col = col_blue)
right_angle(c(1, 0), c(-1, 0), c(0, 1), s = 0.15)
text(3, 0, "a", pos = 1); text(1, 2, "b", pos = 3, col = col_blue)
text(0.5, -0.05, "shadow = 1", pos = 1, col = col_orange, cex = 0.85)
th <- seq(0, atan2(2, 1), length.out = 40); lines(0.5 * cos(th), 0.5 * sin(th))
text(0.6, 0.35, expression(theta), cex = 0.9)








Figure B.5: The inner product as a shadow. The shadow of b on the line through a has length ‖b‖ cos θ = 1, and aᵀb = 3 × 1 = 3.





Everything else follows from this one number:








Quantity
From the inner product
For \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\)




length
\(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}}\)
\(3\) and \(\sqrt 5\)


distance
\(\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\rVert_2\)
\(\sqrt 8\)


angle
\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{y}}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert}\)
\(\cos\theta = \frac{3}{3\sqrt5} \approx 0.447\), so \(\theta \approx 63.4^\circ\)


perpendicular
\(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{y} = 0\)
—





DEF — Two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is zero: the shadow of one on the other has length zero.

Cosine similarity of expression profiles
Read counts are relative: sequencing the same sample twice as deeply roughly doubles every count, while the biology is unchanged. The direction of a count vector is the expression profile; its length mostly reflects sequencing depth. Compare three samples on two genes.


Code
m1 <- c(10, 20); m2 <- c(20, 40); m3 <- c(30, 20)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 45), ylim = c(0, 45), asp = 1, las = 1,
     xlab = "reads on gene 1", ylab = "reads on gene 2")
abline(0, 2, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
arrow(c(0, 0), m2, col = col_blue, lwd = 2); arrow(c(0, 0), m1, col = "black", lwd = 3)
arrow(c(0, 0), m3, col = col_orange, lwd = 2.5)
text(m1[1], m1[2], "sample 1", pos = 2); text(m2[1], m2[2], "sample 2", pos = 4, col = col_blue)
text(m3[1], m3[2], "sample 3", pos = 4, col = col_orange)








Figure B.6: Samples 1 and 2 lie on the same line through the origin: the same profile, sequenced to a different depth. Sample 3 points in another direction. Euclidean distance calls sample 3 the nearer one; the angle says sample 2 has the same profile.






cosine <- function(x, y) sum(x * y) / (sqrt(sum(x^2)) * sqrt(sum(y^2)))
round(rbind(
  euclidean_distance = c(sample2 = sqrt(sum((m2 - m1)^2)), sample3 = sqrt(sum((m3 - m1)^2))),
  cosine_similarity  = c(cosine(m1, m2), cosine(m1, m3)),
  angle_degrees      = acos(pmin(1, c(cosine(m1, m2), cosine(m1, m3)))) * 180 / pi), 3)

#>                    sample2 sample3
#> euclidean_distance  22.361  20.000
#> cosine_similarity    1.000   0.868
#> angle_degrees        0.000  29.745




Correlation is a cosine
One fact links this geometry directly to statistics. Centre two variables by subtracting their means; the cosine of the angle between the centred vectors is their correlation.

set.seed(1)
x <- rnorm(50); y <- 0.6 * x + rnorm(50, 0, 0.8)
c(cosine_of_centred = cosine(x - mean(x), y - mean(y)), correlation = cor(x, y))

#> cosine_of_centred       correlation 
#>         0.5176274         0.5176274




KEY — Centred and orthogonal means uncorrelated. Uncorrelated variables are perpendicular arrows.

↪ Day 3: principal components are chosen perpendicular to each other, and are therefore uncorrelated.







CautionCheck yourself



What is the cosine similarity between a profile \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(5\mathbf{x}\)? And between \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(-\mathbf{x}\)? What does each mean for two expression profiles, and for two centred variables?






TipAnswer





For \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(5\mathbf{x}\) the cosine is \(\frac{5\,\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert \cdot 5\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert} = 1\), an angle of \(0^\circ\): the same profile at another depth. For \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(-\mathbf{x}\) it is \(-1\), an angle of \(180^\circ\). Raw counts are never negative, so this cannot happen for two count profiles. For centred variables, a cosine of \(1\) is a correlation of \(1\) and a cosine of \(-1\) is a perfect negative correlation.

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
section: Projection: the closest point on a line
text:
Projection: the closest point on a line
Here is a question that looks simple. Three standards in a calibration experiment give absorbances \(y = 1, 2, 4\) at concentrations \(c = 0, 1, 2\). No straight line passes through all three points. Which line is best?


Code
cc <- c(0, 1, 2); yy <- c(1, 2, 4)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(cc, yy, pch = 19, cex = 1.3, xlim = c(-0.3, 2.3), ylim = c(0, 4.6), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "concentration c", ylab = "absorbance y", las = 1)
axis(1, at = 0:2); abline(h = 0:4, v = 0:2, col = "grey92")
abline(1, 1, lty = 2, col = col_grey); abline(1, 1.5, lty = 2, col = col_grey)
abline(2 / 3, 1.6, lty = 2, col = col_grey)
points(cc, yy, pch = 19, cex = 1.3)








Figure B.7: Three measurements of a calibration line. No straight line passes through all three points. Which line is the best?





To answer it, start with the simplest version: the point on a line closest to a given point. The line through \(\mathbf{b}\) consists of all multiples \(t\mathbf{b}\). The closest point to \(\mathbf{a}\) is the foot of the perpendicular, the projection:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{b} = \frac{3}{5}\,(1, 2) = (0.6,\ 1.2) .
\]
What is left over, \(\mathbf{a} - \hat{\mathbf{a}} = (2.4, -1.2)\), is perpendicular to the line: its inner product with \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(2.4 - 2.4 = 0\).


Code
p_hat <- sum(a_vec * b_vec) / sum(b_vec^2) * b_vec
par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1))
plane(c(-0.6, 3.6), c(-0.8, 3))
abline(0, 2, col = col_blue, lwd = 1.2)
segments(a_vec[1], a_vec[2], b_vec[1], b_vec[2], lty = 2, col = col_grey)
arrow(c(0, 0), a_vec, col = "black"); arrow(c(0, 0), p_hat, col = col_blue, lwd = 4)
arrow(p_hat, a_vec, col = col_orange, lwd = 3)
right_angle(p_hat, a_vec - p_hat, -b_vec)
text(3, 0, "a", pos = 1); text(p_hat[1], p_hat[2], "projection (0.6, 1.2)", pos = 2, col = col_blue, cex = 0.85)
text(1.9, 0.75, "residual\n(2.4, -1.2)", pos = 4, col = col_orange, cex = 0.85)
text(1.5, 3, "line through b", col = col_blue, cex = 0.85, pos = 4)








Figure B.8: The projection of a on the line through b (blue) and the residual (orange). The residual is perpendicular to the line, and every other point of the line is further from a.







KEY — The closest point is the one whose residual is perpendicular. “Closest” and “perpendicular” are two descriptions of the same point.

The calibration line is a projection
Now the calibration question. Write all three measurements as one vector \(\mathbf{y} = (1, 2, 4)\) in three-dimensional space. A line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 c\) predicts the vector
\[
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \beta_0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + \beta_1 \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta ,
\]
and as \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) vary, these predictions fill a plane through the origin, the column space of \(\mathbf{X}\). The best line is the point of that plane closest to \(\mathbf{y}\): the projection. Its residual must be perpendicular to both columns of \(\mathbf{X}\),
\[
\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \mathbf{0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} .
\]
These are the normal equations of Day 1, now with a picture.


Code
X3 <- cbind(1, cc)
beta <- solve(t(X3) %*% X3, t(X3) %*% yy); yh <- drop(X3 %*% beta)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(cc, yy, pch = 19, xlim = c(-0.4, 2.3), ylim = c(0, 4.5), xaxt = "n", las = 1,
     xlab = "concentration c", ylab = "absorbance y", main = "the least-squares line")
axis(1, at = 0:2); abline(beta[1], beta[2], col = col_blue, lwd = 2.5)
segments(cc, yy, cc, yh, col = col_orange, lwd = 3.5); points(cc, yy, pch = 19)
text(cc, (yy + yh) / 2, c("1/6", "-1/3", "1/6"), pos = c(2, 4, 2), col = col_orange, cex = 0.85)

cross <- function(p, q) c(p[2] * q[3] - p[3] * q[2], p[3] * q[1] - p[1] * q[3], p[1] * q[2] - p[2] * q[1])
nrm <- c(1, -2, 1) / sqrt(6); e1 <- yh / sqrt(sum(yh^2)); e2 <- cross(e1, nrm)
az <- -25 * pi / 180; el <- 18 * pi / 180
rgt <- -sin(az) * e1 + cos(az) * e2
upv <- sin(el) * (cos(az) * e1 + sin(az) * e2) + cos(el) * nrm
scr <- function(v) c(sum(v * rgt), sum(v * upv))
pl <- rbind(scr(-0.3 * e1 - 1.3 * e2), scr(5 * e1 - 1.3 * e2), scr(5 * e1 + 1.3 * e2), scr(-0.3 * e1 + 1.3 * e2))
plot(NA, xlim = range(pl[, 1]), ylim = range(pl[, 2]) + c(-0.1, 0.45), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "the same fit in the data space")
polygon(pl, col = "#DCE6F1", border = "grey60")
sy <- scr(yy); sh <- scr(yh)
arrow(c(0, 0), scr(X3[, 1]), col = "grey40", lwd = 2); arrow(c(0, 0), scr(X3[, 2]), col = "grey40", lwd = 2)
arrow(c(0, 0), sh, col = col_blue, lwd = 3); arrow(c(0, 0), sy, col = "black", lwd = 3)
arrow(sh, sy, col = col_orange, lwd = 3)
text(sy[1], sy[2], expression(bold(y)), pos = 3); text(sh[1], sh[2], expression(hat(bold(y))), pos = 4, col = col_blue)
text(pl[2, 1], pl[2, 2], "column space of X", pos = 2, col = col_blue, cex = 0.8, offset = 1.5)








Figure B.9: The same least-squares fit seen twice. Left: the usual picture, with the residuals as vertical segments. Right: the data space ℝ³, one axis per measurement. The predictions of all possible lines form a plane (the column space of X); the fitted vector ŷ is the projection of y onto it, and the residual vector is perpendicular to the plane.






X3 <- cbind(intercept = 1, c = cc)
beta_hat <- solve(t(X3) %*% X3, t(X3) %*% yy)
res <- yy - drop(X3 %*% beta_hat)

list(beta = drop(beta_hat), residuals = res,
     residual_dot_columns = drop(t(X3) %*% res),
     lm = coef(lm(yy ~ cc)))

#> $beta
#> intercept         c 
#> 0.8333333 1.5000000 
#> 
#> $residuals
#> [1]  0.1666667 -0.3333333  0.1666667
#> 
#> $residual_dot_columns
#>     intercept             c 
#> -3.330669e-16 -4.440892e-16 
#> 
#> $lm
#> (Intercept)          cc 
#>   0.8333333   1.5000000


The best line is \(\hat y = \tfrac56 + \tfrac32 c\), with residuals \(\tfrac16\), \(-\tfrac13\) and \(\tfrac16\), and the residual vector is perpendicular to both columns.


KEY — Least squares is a projection. The fitted values are the shadow of the data on the space of everything the model can produce; the residuals are what sticks out perpendicular to it.

↪ Day 1 derived the same solution with derivatives. Days 5 and 7 use this picture to explain degrees of freedom and leave-one-out cross-validation; Appendix C gives the details.







CautionCheck yourself



Without computing, explain why the residuals of any regression with an intercept add up to zero. (Hint: the residual vector is perpendicular to every column of \(\mathbf{X}\). What is the first column?)






TipAnswer





The first column of \(\mathbf{X}\) is \((1, 1, \dots, 1)\). The residual vector is perpendicular to it, so its inner product with that column, which is the sum of the residuals, is zero. For the calibration line: \(\tfrac16 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac16 = 0\).
crumbs: B  Linear algebra: the geometry of data

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
text:
A matrix deforms space
Multiplying by a matrix moves every point of the plane. The matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) sends the basis vectors \((1, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\) to its own columns, \((2, 0)\) and \((1, 2)\), and drags the whole grid along: squares become parallelograms, and the unit circle becomes an ellipse.


Code
draw_grid <- function(T, col = "grey85") {
  for (k in -4:6) {
    s <- seq(-4, 6, length.out = 2)
    l1 <- T %*% rbind(k, s); l2 <- T %*% rbind(s, k)
    lines(l1[1, ], l1[2, ], col = col); lines(l2[1, ], l2[2, ], col = col)
  }
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
plane(c(-2.5, 7), c(-2.5, 5), grid = FALSE, main = "before")
draw_grid(diag(2)); lines(u, col = col_green, lwd = 2.5)
arrow(c(0, 0), a_vec); arrow(c(0, 0), b_vec, col = col_blue)
text(3, 0, "a", pos = 1); text(1, 2, "b", pos = 2, col = col_blue)

plane(c(-2.5, 7), c(-2.5, 5), grid = FALSE, main = "after multiplying by M")
draw_grid(M_mat); Mu <- u %*% t(M_mat); lines(Mu, col = col_green, lwd = 2.5)
Ma <- drop(M_mat %*% a_vec); Mb <- drop(M_mat %*% b_vec)
arrow(c(0, 0), Ma); arrow(c(0, 0), Mb, col = col_blue)
text(Ma[1], Ma[2], "Ma", pos = 1); text(Mb[1], Mb[2], "Mb", pos = 4, col = col_blue)








Figure B.10: Left: the plane, with a grid and the unit circle. Right: the same plane after multiplying every point by M. The grid is stretched and sheared, the circle has become an ellipse, and a and b are mapped to Ma = (6, 0) and Mb = (4, 4).







DEF — \(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\) is a weighted sum of the columns of \(\mathbf{M}\), with the coordinates of \(\mathbf{x}\) as weights. The columns show where the basis vectors go.

Measuring with a different ruler
The length of \(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\) can be computed without first deforming the plane:
\[
\lVert\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\rVert^2 = (\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top\underbrace{\mathbf{M}^\top\mathbf{M}}_{\mathbf{A}}\,\mathbf{x} .
\]
So there are two equivalent pictures. Either deform the plane with \(\mathbf{M}\) and measure with an ordinary ruler, or leave the plane alone and measure with the matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), whose “circle”, the set of points with \(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 1\), is an ellipse.


Code
EA <- ellipse_A(A_mat)
par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1))
plane(c(-1, 3.4), c(-1, 2.4))
lines(u, lty = 2, col = col_grey); lines(EA, col = col_orange, lwd = 2.5)
arrow(c(0, 0), a_vec); arrow(c(0, 0), b_vec, col = col_blue)
points(rbind(a_vec / 6, b_vec / sqrt(32)), pch = 19, col = col_orange)
text(3, 0, "a: A-length 6", pos = 3, cex = 0.85)
text(1, 2, expression(paste("b: A-length ", sqrt(32))), pos = 4, cex = 0.85, col = col_blue)








Figure B.11: The vectors with A-length 1 form an ellipse (orange); the ordinary unit circle is dashed. Measured with A, the arrow a is 6 units long, because the ellipse fits into it six times. The ellipse is narrow along a, so a is long in this ruler.






A_len <- function(x) sqrt(drop(t(x) %*% A_mat %*% x))
rbind(via_A    = c(a = A_len(a_vec), b = A_len(b_vec)),
      via_M    = c(sqrt(sum((M_mat %*% a_vec)^2)), sqrt(sum((M_mat %*% b_vec)^2))))

#>       a        b
#> via_A 6 5.656854
#> via_M 6 5.656854


This is more than a curiosity. It appears twice later in the course.

Mahalanobis distance (Day 4) measures with \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{S}^{-1}\), the inverse of the covariance matrix of the data. Its unit “circle” has the shape of the data cloud, so a step along the direction in which the data vary a lot counts as short.
\(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\), which appears in every least-squares formula, has the form \(\mathbf{M}^\top\mathbf{M}\). The contours of the residual sum of squares in the regularisation picture above are exactly such ellipses.



KEY — A symmetric matrix of the form \(\mathbf{M}^\top\mathbf{M}\) defines a ruler whose unit ball is an ellipse. Appendix C shows which matrices may be used this way (the positive definite ones).






CautionCheck yourself



Compute the A-length of \(\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)\) and of \(\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1)\), using only the diagonal of \(\mathbf{A}\). Which of the two directions does the ellipse reach further in?






TipAnswer





\(\mathbf{e}_1^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_1 = a_{11} = 4\), so \(\mathbf{e}_1\) has A-length \(2\); \(\mathbf{e}_2^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2 = a_{22} = 5\), so \(\mathbf{e}_2\) has A-length \(\sqrt 5 \approx 2.24\). A vector that is long in this ruler is one into which the ellipse fits many times, so the ellipse reaches less far along \(\mathbf{e}_2\): it crosses the axes at \(\tfrac12\) horizontally and at \(1/\sqrt5 \approx 0.45\) vertically.
crumbs: B  Linear algebra: the geometry of data

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
text:
Rotations and new axes
Some matrices deform nothing. A rotation turns the plane without stretching it, so lengths and angles are unchanged. Its columns are perpendicular vectors of length one, which is written \(\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}\).


Code
Qr <- matrix(c(0, 1, -1, 0), 2)                # rotation over 90 degrees
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
plane(c(-2.5, 6.5), c(-1, 4.5), main = "rotation Q: nothing deformed")
for (v in list(a_vec, b_vec)) arrow(c(0, 0), v, col = "grey75", lty = 3)
arrow(c(0, 0), Qr %*% a_vec); arrow(c(0, 0), Qr %*% b_vec, col = col_blue)
text(0, 3, "Qa", pos = 4); text(-2, 1, "Qb", pos = 3, col = col_blue)
plane(c(-2.5, 6.5), c(-1, 4.5), main = "deformation M")
for (v in list(a_vec, b_vec)) arrow(c(0, 0), v, col = "grey75", lty = 3)
arrow(c(0, 0), Ma); arrow(c(0, 0), Mb, col = col_blue)
text(Ma[1], Ma[2], "Ma", pos = 1); text(Mb[1], Mb[2], "Mb", pos = 4, col = col_blue)








Figure B.12: Left: rotating a and b over 90° keeps their lengths (3 and √5) and the angle between them (63.4°). Right: the deformation M changes both; Ma and Mb make an angle of 45°.





Two perpendicular unit vectors form an orthonormal basis: a new pair of axes. Take \(\mathbf{q}_1 = (0.6, 0.8)\) and \(\mathbf{q}_2 = (-0.8, 0.6)\). The coordinates of \(\mathbf{b}\) on the new axes are simply its shadows on them:
\[
\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{q}_1 = 0.6 + 1.6 = 2.2,
\qquad
\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{q}_2 = -0.8 + 1.2 = 0.4,
\qquad
\mathbf{b} = 2.2\,\mathbf{q}_1 + 0.4\,\mathbf{q}_2 .
\]


Code
q1 <- c(0.6, 0.8); q2 <- c(-0.8, 0.6)
par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1))
plane(c(-1.2, 2.4), c(-0.4, 2.4))
abline(0, 0.8 / 0.6, col = "grey80"); abline(0, -0.6 / 0.8, col = "grey80")
s1 <- sum(b_vec * q1) * q1; s2 <- sum(b_vec * q2) * q2
arrow(c(0, 0), s1, col = col_orange, lwd = 2); arrow(s1, b_vec, col = col_orange, lwd = 2)
arrow(c(0, 0), q1, col = col_green, lwd = 3); arrow(c(0, 0), q2, col = col_green, lwd = 3)
arrow(c(0, 0), b_vec, col = col_blue, lwd = 3)
right_angle(c(0, 0), q1, q2, s = 0.15)
text(q1[1], q1[2], expression(q[1]), pos = 4, col = col_green)
text(q2[1], q2[2], expression(q[2]), pos = 2, col = col_green)
text(1, 2, "b", pos = 3, col = col_blue)
text(s1[1], s1[2], "2.2 q1", pos = 4, col = col_orange, cex = 0.85)








Figure B.13: Coordinates on new perpendicular axes are shadows. The basis vectors q₁ and q₂ (green) are perpendicular and of length 1. The vector b is the sum of its shadow on q₁ (2.2 q₁) and its shadow on q₂ (0.4 q₂).







KEY — In an orthonormal basis, a coordinate is a shadow: one inner product, no system of equations to solve.

↪ Day 3: PCA chooses new orthonormal axes for the data cloud. The scores are the shadows of the samples on those axes, and the loadings are the axes themselves.







CautionCheck yourself



Verify that the coordinates \(2.2\) and \(0.4\) give back a vector of length \(\sqrt5\). Why is that guaranteed?






TipAnswer





\(\sqrt{2.2^2 + 0.4^2} = \sqrt{4.84 + 0.16} = \sqrt5\). Because the new axes are perpendicular and of length one, Pythagoras applies in the new coordinates exactly as in the old ones. Changing to an orthonormal basis is a rotation (or reflection), and a rotation does not change lengths.
crumbs: B  Linear algebra: the geometry of data

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
section: Eigenvectors: the axes of a data cloud
text:
Eigenvectors: the axes of a data cloud
Most directions are turned by a matrix. A few special directions are only stretched: these are the eigenvectors, and the stretch factors are the eigenvalues,
\[
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} .
\]
For a symmetric matrix such as \(\mathbf{A}\) the eigenvectors are perpendicular, and they are the axes of its ellipse.


Code
ev <- eigen(A_mat)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
plane(c(-6.5, 6.5), c(-6.5, 6.5), grid = FALSE, main = "what A does to directions")
for (k in 0:7) {
  v <- c(cos(k * pi / 8), sin(k * pi / 8)); Av <- drop(A_mat %*% v)
  arrow(c(0, 0), v, col = "grey60", lwd = 1.5); arrow(c(0, 0), Av, col = "grey20", lwd = 1.2)
}
for (j in 1:2) {
  v <- ev$vectors[, j]; arrow(c(0, 0), ev$values[j] * v, col = col_green, lwd = 3)
}
plane(c(-6.5, 6.5), c(-6.5, 6.5), grid = FALSE, main = "the axes of the ellipse")
lines(u %*% t(A_mat), col = col_orange, lwd = 2.5); lines(u, lty = 2, col = col_grey)
for (j in 1:2) arrow(c(0, 0), ev$values[j] * ev$vectors[, j], col = col_green, lwd = 3)
text(ev$values[1] * ev$vectors[1, 1], ev$values[1] * ev$vectors[2, 1],
     bquote(lambda == .(round(ev$values[1], 2))), pos = 4, col = col_green, cex = 0.85)
text(ev$values[2] * ev$vectors[1, 2], ev$values[2] * ev$vectors[2, 2],
     bquote(lambda == .(round(ev$values[2], 2))), pos = 2, col = col_green, cex = 0.85)








Figure B.14: Left: A acting on unit vectors in eight directions (grey: before, black: after). Most directions are turned; the two eigenvector directions (green) are only stretched. Right: the eigenvectors are the axes of the ellipse that A makes of the unit circle.






Why this matters for data
The covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) of a data cloud is symmetric, and its eigenvectors have a statistical meaning. Project the centred data onto a unit direction \(\mathbf{w}\); the variance of the projected values is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\text{scores along }\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{w} .
\]
Let the direction turn through a half circle and record that variance.


Code
set.seed(5)
D  <- MASS::mvrnorm(300, c(0, 0), Sigma = A_mat)
Sd <- cov(D); es <- eigen(Sd)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plane(c(-7, 7), c(-7, 7), grid = FALSE, main = "a data cloud and its axes",
      xlab = "gene 1 (centred)", ylab = "gene 2 (centred)")
points(D, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor(col_blue, 0.35), cex = 0.7)
for (j in 1:2) arrow(c(0, 0), 2 * sqrt(es$values[j]) * es$vectors[, j], col = col_green, lwd = 3)
ang  <- seq(0, pi, length.out = 361)
vdir <- sapply(ang, function(t) { w <- c(cos(t), sin(t)); drop(t(w) %*% Sd %*% w) })
plot(ang * 180 / pi, vdir, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = col_blue, las = 1,
     xlab = "direction (degrees)", ylab = "variance along the direction",
     main = "variance as the direction turns")
abline(h = es$values, lty = 2, col = col_green)
pc_angle <- (atan2(es$vectors[2, 1], es$vectors[1, 1]) * 180 / pi) %% 180
abline(v = pc_angle, lty = 3)
text(95, es$values + c(-0.2, 0.2), c("largest eigenvalue", "smallest eigenvalue"), adj = 0.5, cex = 0.8, col = col_green)








Figure B.15: Left: 300 simulated samples on two genes, with the eigenvectors of their covariance matrix (green), each drawn with length 2√λ. Right: the variance of the data projected onto a direction, as the direction turns. The maximum is the largest eigenvalue, reached at the first eigenvector; the minimum is the smallest eigenvalue, at the second.






c(max_variance = max(vdir), largest_eigenvalue = es$values[1],
  min_variance = min(vdir), smallest_eigenvalue = es$values[2])

#>        max_variance  largest_eigenvalue        min_variance smallest_eigenvalue 
#>            6.326135            6.326162            2.538156            2.538129




KEY — For a covariance matrix, an eigenvector is a direction of extreme variance, and its eigenvalue is that variance. The first eigenvector is the direction in which the data vary most.

↪ This is principal component analysis (Day 3). Day 3 derives the result; Appendix C shows how eigenvectors are computed.







CautionCheck yourself



The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\) are about \(6.56\) and \(2.44\). Their sum is \(9\), which is also \(a_{11} + a_{22} = 4 + 5\). If \(\mathbf{A}\) were a covariance matrix, what would this sum mean?






TipAnswer





The diagonal of a covariance matrix holds the variances of the variables, so \(4 + 5\) is the total variance. The eigenvalues are the variances along the new perpendicular axes, and they add up to the same total. Rotating to new axes redistributes the variance without changing the total. Day 3 uses this to say how much of the total variance each principal component explains: here \(6.56/9 \approx 73\%\) along the first eigenvector.
crumbs: B  Linear algebra: the geometry of data

title: Appendix B — Linear algebra: the geometry of data
section: The singular value decomposition, and why ridge regression works
text:
The singular value decomposition, and why ridge regression works
Every data matrix, of any shape, can be written as a rotation, a stretch along perpendicular axes, and another rotation:
\[
\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\top .
\]
The columns of \(\mathbf{V}\) are the axes of the data cloud (the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\)), and the singular values \(d_j\) on the diagonal of \(\mathbf{D}\) measure the spread along each axis: \(d_j^2\) is an eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\).
This decomposition explains what goes wrong with least squares when predictors are correlated, and how ridge regression repairs it. Least squares divides by \(d_j^2\) along each axis. A direction in which the data hardly vary has a tiny \(d_j\), and dividing by it blows up the estimate. Ridge regression divides by \(d_j^2 + \lambda\) instead, which shrinks the fit along axis \(j\) by the factor
\[
\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda} .
\]


Code
lam <- 10^seq(-2, 3, length.out = 200)
dvals <- c(10, 3, 1, 0.3)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = range(lam), ylim = c(0, 1), log = "x", las = 1,
     xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "fraction of the fit that is kept")
cols <- c(col_blue, col_green, col_orange, "firebrick")
for (k in seq_along(dvals)) lines(lam, dvals[k]^2 / (dvals[k]^2 + lam), lwd = 2.5, col = cols[k])
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2.5, col = cols, legend = paste("d =", dvals), cex = 0.85)








Figure B.16: Ridge regression shrinks the fit along each axis of the data by the factor d²/(d² + λ). Directions with much spread (large d) are hardly shrunk; directions with little spread, the unstable combinations of correlated predictors, are shrunk most.






s <- svd(scale(D, scale = FALSE))
round(rbind(from_svd = s$d^2 / (nrow(D) - 1), eigenvalues_of_S = es$values), 4)

#>                    [,1]   [,2]
#> from_svd         6.3262 2.5381
#> eigenvalues_of_S 6.3262 2.5381




KEY — Ridge regression keeps the directions in which the data carry information and suppresses the directions in which they do not.

↪ Day 9: ridge regression, the lasso, PCR and PLS all act on these axes in different ways.







CautionCheck yourself



With \(\lambda = 1\), what fraction of the fit is kept along an axis with \(d = 10\), and along an axis with \(d = 0.3\)? What does that say about which information ridge regression gives up?






TipAnswer





For \(d = 10\): \(100/101 \approx 0.99\), almost everything is kept. For \(d = 0.3\): \(0.09/1.09 \approx 0.08\), less than a tenth is kept. Ridge regression gives up mainly the directions along which the predictors hardly vary. Those are exactly the directions in which least squares is most unstable, so a small bias buys a large reduction in variance.

text:
Reading
ISLR assumes this material. The sections above are the background for §6.2 and §6.3 (regularisation and dimension reduction) and §12.2 (principal components). For the formal side, see Appendix C and Mathematics for Machine Learning by Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong, Chapters 2 to 4.

title: Appendix C — Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms
text:
Norms and inner products
This appendix gives the formal side of Appendix B. That appendix builds intuition from pictures; here the same ideas are stated as definitions and theorems, a few are proved, and the algorithms that software uses are written out in R. The numbering (Definition C.1, Theorem C.2, …) is for reference.
The Lp norms \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_p = \big(\sum_j |x_j|^p\big)^{1/p}\) satisfy these rules for \(p \ge 1\), and \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty = \max_j |x_j|\) is the limit as \(p \to \infty\). For \(0 < p < 1\) the triangle inequality fails: the “unit ball” is no longer convex, which is why the lasso uses \(p = 1\), the smallest \(p\) that still gives a norm.
Proof. The first inequality holds because \(\max_j x_j^2 \le \sum_j x_j^2\). For the second, \(\big(\sum_j |x_j|\big)^2 = \sum_j x_j^2 + \sum_{j \ne k} |x_j||x_k| \ge \sum_j x_j^2\). The third is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Theorem C.4) applied to \((|x_1|, \dots, |x_p|)\) and \((1, \dots, 1)\). \(\square\)
In the pictures: the square contains the circle, which contains the diamond.
The L2 norm comes from an inner product; the L1 and L∞ norms do not. That is why only L2 has angles and projections.
Proof. If \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}\) both sides are zero. Otherwise, for every number \(t\), \[
0 \le \lVert\mathbf{x} - t\mathbf{y}\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert^2 - 2t\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle + t^2\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^2 .
\] Choose \(t = \langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle / \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^2\), the coefficient of the projection of \(\mathbf{x}\) onto \(\mathbf{y}\). Then the right-hand side is \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert^2 - \langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle^2 / \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^2\), and rearranging gives the inequality. Equality means \(\mathbf{x} - t\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}\). \(\square\)
The proof is the picture of the shadow: the residual of a projection has non-negative length. The theorem guarantees that \(\cos\theta = \langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle / (\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert)\) lies between \(-1\) and \(1\), so angles, cosine similarities and correlations are well defined.
Proof. \(\lVert\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert^2 + 2\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle + \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^2 \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert^2 + 2\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert + \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^2 = (\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert + \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert)^2\), using Cauchy–Schwarz. \(\square\)
crumbs: C  Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms

title: Appendix C — Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms
text:
NoteDefinition C.1 — Norm



A norm on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is a function \(\mathbf{x} \mapsto \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\) with, for all vectors \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\) and numbers \(c\):

\(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert \ge 0\), with equality only for \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) (positivity);
\(\lVert c\,\mathbf{x}\rVert = |c|\,\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\) (scaling);
\(\lVert\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}\rVert \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert + \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert\) (triangle inequality).










NoteTheorem C.2 — Comparing norms



For every \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^p\), \[
\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_1 \le \sqrt{p}\,\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 .
\]










NoteDefinition C.3 — Inner product



An inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is a function \(\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle\) that is

symmetric: \(\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle = \langle\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}\rangle\);
linear in each argument: \(\langle c\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{y}\rangle = c\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle + \langle\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{y}\rangle\);
positive definite: \(\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}\rangle > 0\) for \(\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}\).

Every inner product defines a norm, \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert = \sqrt{\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}\rangle}\). The standard inner product is \(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{y}\).









NoteTheorem C.4 — Cauchy–Schwarz inequality



For every inner product, \(|\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle| \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert\), with equality exactly when one vector is a multiple of the other.










NoteTheorem C.5 — Triangle inequality



For a norm that comes from an inner product, \(\lVert\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}\rVert \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert + \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert\).
crumbs: C  Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms

title: Appendix C — Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms
text:
The A-inner product






NoteDefinition C.6 — Positive definite matrix



A symmetric \(p \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is positive definite if \(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} > 0\) for every \(\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}\), and positive semi-definite if \(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \ge 0\).








NoteTheorem C.7 — The A-inner product



If \(\mathbf{A}\) is positive definite, then \(\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle_{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) is an inner product. Conversely, every inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) has this form for some positive definite \(\mathbf{A}\), namely \(a_{jk} = \langle\mathbf{e}_j, \mathbf{e}_k\rangle\).


Proof. Symmetry follows from \(\mathbf{A}^\top = \mathbf{A}\), linearity from the rules of matrix multiplication, and positivity is the definition of positive definite. For the converse, write \(\mathbf{x} = \sum_j x_j\mathbf{e}_j\) and \(\mathbf{y} = \sum_k y_k\mathbf{e}_k\) and use linearity: \(\langle\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle = \sum_{j,k} x_j y_k \langle\mathbf{e}_j, \mathbf{e}_k\rangle = \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\). \(\square\)






NoteTheorem C.8 — Which matrices are positive definite



For a symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) the following are equivalent:

\(\mathbf{A}\) is positive definite;
all eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\) are positive;
\(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{M}^\top\mathbf{M}\) for some invertible matrix \(\mathbf{M}\).

For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, (1) holds exactly when \(a_{11} > 0\) and \(\det\mathbf{A} > 0\).


Proof sketch. (3 ⇒ 1): \(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{M}^\top\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x} = \lVert\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\rVert^2 > 0\) for \(\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}\), because \(\mathbf{M}\) is invertible. (1 ⇒ 2): for a unit eigenvector, \(\lambda = \mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} > 0\). (2 ⇒ 3): with the spectral theorem (C.11), \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{V}^\top\); take \(\mathbf{M} = \boldsymbol\Lambda^{1/2}\mathbf{V}^\top\). \(\square\)
The matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) in (3) is not unique. Software uses the Cholesky factorisation, in which \(\mathbf{M}\) is upper triangular; R computes it with chol(). The chapter’s matrix \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) has \(a_{11} = 4 > 0\) and \(\det\mathbf{A} = 16 > 0\), and its Cholesky factor is exactly the \(\mathbf{M}\) of the chapter:

A <- matrix(c(4, 2, 2, 5), 2)
chol(A)

#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    2    1
#> [2,]    0    2

eigen(A)$values

#> [1] 6.561553 2.438447


Consequences used in the course:

\(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is always positive semi-definite, and positive definite exactly when the columns of \(\mathbf{X}\) are linearly independent. Least squares has a unique solution precisely then.
\(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}\) has eigenvalues \(d_j^2 + \lambda > 0\), so it is positive definite for every \(\lambda > 0\). That is why ridge regression always has a unique solution (Day 9).
A covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is positive semi-definite, because \(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{w}\) is a variance. If it is positive definite, \(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\) is too, and \(\sqrt{(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})^\top\mathbf{S}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})}\) is the Mahalanobis distance (Day 4).

title: Appendix C — Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms
text:
Projection






NoteTheorem C.9 — Projection onto a column space



Let \(\mathbf{X}\) be \(n \times p\) with linearly independent columns. For every \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) there is exactly one vector \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) in the column space of \(\mathbf{X}\) that is closest to \(\mathbf{y}\). It is characterised by the normal equations \[
\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \mathbf{0}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} .
\]


Proof. Let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) satisfy the normal equations and let \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) be any other point of the column space. The residual \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) is perpendicular to every column, hence to \(\mathbf{X}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} - \boldsymbol\beta)\). By Pythagoras, \[
\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert^2 + \lVert\mathbf{X}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} - \boldsymbol\beta)\rVert^2 \ge \lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert^2 ,
\] with equality only when \(\mathbf{X}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} - \boldsymbol\beta) = \mathbf{0}\), that is \(\boldsymbol\beta = \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). The matrix \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is invertible by Theorem C.8. \(\square\)
The rest of this section uses a real regression to check the theory.

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
X   <- model.matrix(fit)
y   <- mtcars$mpg

beta <- solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% y)
cbind(by_hand = drop(beta), lm = coef(fit))

#>                 by_hand          lm
#> (Intercept) 37.22727012 37.22727012
#> wt          -3.87783074 -3.87783074
#> hp          -0.03177295 -0.03177295

round(t(X) %*% resid(fit), 8)   # the residuals are orthogonal to every column

#>             [,1]
#> (Intercept)    0
#> wt             0
#> hp             0



The hat matrix
Substituting \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) shows that the fitted values are a linear function of the observations:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \underbrace{\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top}_{\mathbf{H}}\,\mathbf{y} .
\]






NoteTheorem C.10 — Properties of the hat matrix



The hat matrix \(\mathbf{H}\), the projection onto the column space of \(\mathbf{X}\), satisfies

\(\mathbf{H}^\top = \mathbf{H}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{H}\): projecting twice changes nothing;
\(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = p\), the number of columns;
\(0 \le h_{ii} \le 1\); the diagonal element \(h_{ii}\) is the leverage of observation \(i\), how strongly it determines its own fitted value.



Proof of 2. Using \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{BC}) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{CB})\): \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = \operatorname{tr}\big((\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\big) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{I}_p) = p\). \(\square\)

H <- X %*% solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X)
c(trace        = sum(diag(H)),
  HH_minus_H   = max(abs(H %*% H - H)),
  vs_hatvalues = max(abs(diag(H) - hatvalues(fit))))

#>        trace   HH_minus_H vs_hatvalues 
#> 3.000000e+00 1.526557e-15 1.582068e-15




↪ Day 5 uses \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = p\) to explain the penalty in AIC; Day 7 uses the leverages \(h_{ii}\) for a shortcut to leave-one-out cross-validation; Day 9 uses the trace to define the effective degrees of freedom of ridge regression.


How lm computes: the QR decomposition
The formula \((\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\) is how least squares is derived, not how it is computed. Forming \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) squares the condition number, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, which measures how strongly rounding errors are amplified.

c(kappa_X = kappa(X, exact = TRUE), kappa_XtX = kappa(t(X) %*% X, exact = TRUE))

#>     kappa_X   kappa_XtX 
#>    587.7103 345403.3511


lm factorises \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}\), with orthonormal columns in \(\mathbf{Q}\) and an upper-triangular \(\mathbf{R}\). The normal equations then collapse to
\[
\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{R}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{y}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf{R}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{y} ,
\]
a triangular system solved by back-substitution. The Gram–Schmidt algorithm builds \(\mathbf{Q}\) one column at a time with the projections of Appendix B: from each column of \(\mathbf{X}\), subtract its shadows on the columns already processed, then scale what is left to length one.

gram_schmidt <- function(X) {
  Q <- X
  R <- matrix(0, ncol(X), ncol(X))
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X))) {
    v <- X[, j]
    for (i in seq_len(j - 1)) {
      R[i, j] <- sum(Q[, i] * v)        # shadow on an earlier direction
      v <- v - R[i, j] * Q[, i]         # remove that projection
    }
    R[j, j] <- sqrt(sum(v^2))
    Q[, j]  <- v / R[j, j]              # normalise the residual
  }
  list(Q = Q, R = R)
}

qr_X <- gram_schmidt(X)
round(t(qr_X$Q) %*% qr_X$Q, 10)       # orthonormal columns

#>             (Intercept) wt hp
#> (Intercept)           1  0  0
#> wt                    0  1  0
#> hp                    0  0  1

cbind(qr = drop(backsolve(qr_X$R, t(qr_X$Q) %*% y)), lm = coef(fit))

#>                      qr          lm
#> (Intercept) 37.22727012 37.22727012
#> wt          -3.87783074 -3.87783074
#> hp          -0.03177295 -0.03177295




DEF — Column \(j\) of \(\mathbf{Q}\) is the residual of predictor \(j\) after projecting onto the earlier predictors. That is why a regression coefficient measures the effect of a predictor after adjusting for the others.
Production code uses Householder reflections, a numerically more stable route to the same factorisation.


Least squares by gradient descent
A third route needs no factorisation, and it is the route machine learning takes when a problem has no formula. The residual sum of squares \(\text{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta) = \lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2\) has gradient \(-2\,\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\), and gradient descent repeatedly takes a small step downhill:
\[
\boldsymbol\beta \leftarrow \boldsymbol\beta + \eta\,\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta).
\]
The iteration converges only if \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\), with \(\lambda_{\max}\) the largest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\), and it converges slowly when the eigenvalues are very unequal, that is when the RSS ellipses of Appendix B are long and narrow.

Zs <- cbind(1, scale(mtcars[, c("wt", "hp")]))    # standardised predictors

grad_descent <- function(Z, y, eta, iters) {
  b <- rep(0, ncol(Z))
  for (i in seq_len(iters)) b <- b + eta * drop(t(Z) %*% (y - Z %*% b))
  b
}
l_max <- max(eigen(t(Zs) %*% Zs)$values)

rbind(after_10    = grad_descent(Zs, y, 1 / l_max, 10),
      after_200   = grad_descent(Zs, y, 1 / l_max, 200),
      exact       = coef(lm(y ~ Zs - 1)),
      eta_too_big = grad_descent(Zs, y, 2.1 / l_max, 50))

#>                              wt         hp
#> after_10    20.08944  -3.713558  -2.259179
#> after_200   20.09062  -3.794292  -2.178444
#> exact       20.09062  -3.794292  -2.178444
#> eta_too_big 20.09063 346.778037 348.393885


With a suitable step the iteration reaches the least-squares solution; with a step slightly too large it diverges. Standardising the predictors makes the eigenvalues more equal and the ellipses rounder, which speeds convergence: one reason machine-learning methods so often require scaled inputs.


↪ Day 6 fits logistic regression with Newton’s method, a close relative. Day 10 shows that boosting is gradient descent in a space of functions.

title: Appendix C — Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms
text:
Symmetric matrices and eigenvectors






NoteTheorem C.11 — Spectral theorem



A real symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) has real eigenvalues, and its eigenvectors can be chosen perpendicular and of unit length. With the eigenvectors as the columns of \(\mathbf{V}\) and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\), \[
\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{V}^\top, \qquad \mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I} .
\]


Why the eigenvectors are perpendicular. If \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1\) and \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2\) with \(\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2\), then \(\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1^\top\mathbf{v}_2 = (\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}_1)^\top\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{v}_1^\top\mathbf{v}_2\), so \((\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)\,\mathbf{v}_1^\top\mathbf{v}_2 = 0\) and \(\mathbf{v}_1^\top\mathbf{v}_2 = 0\). \(\square\)
For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix the eigenvalues solve the characteristic equation \(\lambda^2 - \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A})\lambda + \det(\mathbf{A}) = 0\). For the chapter’s \(\mathbf{A}\) this is \(\lambda^2 - 9\lambda + 16 = 0\), so \(\lambda = (9 \pm \sqrt{17})/2 \approx 6.56\) and \(2.44\).






NoteTheorem C.12 — Eigenvectors maximise variance (Rayleigh quotient)



Let \(\mathbf{S}\) be symmetric with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_p\). Over all unit vectors \(\mathbf{w}\), \[
\max_{\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 1} \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{w} = \lambda_1 ,
\qquad
\min_{\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 1} \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{w} = \lambda_p ,
\] attained at the corresponding eigenvectors.


Proof. Write \(\mathbf{w} = \sum_j c_j\mathbf{v}_j\) in the orthonormal eigenvector basis; then \(\sum_j c_j^2 = 1\) and \(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{w} = \sum_j \lambda_j c_j^2\), a weighted average of the eigenvalues. A weighted average is at most the largest and at least the smallest value, with equality when all weight is on one eigenvector. \(\square\)
This is the variance-as-the-direction-turns curve of Appendix B, and the theorem behind PCA (Day 3).

Xc <- scale(as.matrix(iris[, 1:4]), center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
S  <- t(Xc) %*% Xc / (nrow(Xc) - 1)
e  <- eigen(S)
Z  <- Xc %*% e$vectors           # rotate the data onto the eigenvectors

round(cov(Z), 4)                 # the covariances have gone

#>        [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]
#> [1,] 4.2282 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000
#> [2,] 0.0000 0.2427 0.0000 0.0000
#> [3,] 0.0000 0.0000 0.0782 0.0000
#> [4,] 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0238

c(trace = sum(diag(S)), sum_eigenvalues = sum(e$values))

#>           trace sum_eigenvalues 
#>        4.572957        4.572957



Computing eigenvectors: power iteration
The characteristic equation is a hand method for \(2 \times 2\) matrices. For twenty thousand genes software works iteratively. The simplest algorithm is power iteration: start from any vector, multiply by \(\mathbf{S}\), rescale to length one, and repeat. Writing the start as \(\mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p\),
\[
\mathbf{S}^t\mathbf{v} = \lambda_1^t\Big(c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\big(\tfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\big)^t\mathbf{v}_2 + \dots\Big),
\]
and since \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1 < 1\), every term except the first dies out. In the picture of Appendix B: each multiplication turns every direction a little further towards the long axis of the ellipse.

power_iteration <- function(S, iters = 100) {
  v <- rep(1, ncol(S)) / sqrt(ncol(S))
  for (i in seq_len(iters)) {
    v <- S %*% v
    v <- v / sqrt(sum(v^2))
  }
  list(vector = drop(v), value = drop(t(v) %*% S %*% v))
}

p1 <- power_iteration(S)
rbind(power_iteration = c(p1$value, p1$vector),
      eigen           = c(e$values[1], e$vectors[, 1]))

#>                          Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
#> power_iteration 4.228242    0.3613866 -0.08452251    0.8566706   0.3582892
#> eigen           4.228242    0.3613866 -0.08452251    0.8566706   0.3582892


The first column is the eigenvalue, the others the eigenvector (a sign flip would describe the same direction). The next eigenvector is found by deflation: remove the direction just found, and iterate again.

S_deflated <- S - p1$value * p1$vector %*% t(p1$vector)
c(power_iteration = power_iteration(S_deflated)$value, eigen = e$values[2])

#> power_iteration           eigen 
#>       0.2426707       0.2426707




KEY — The leading eigenvector of a covariance matrix can be found with nothing but repeated matrix–vector multiplication. That is why PCA remains feasible on very large data.

title: Appendix C — Linear algebra: definitions, proofs and algorithms
text:
The singular value decomposition






NoteTheorem C.13 — Singular value decomposition



Every \(n \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) can be written as \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\top\), with \(\mathbf{U}\) (\(n \times r\)) and \(\mathbf{V}\) (\(p \times r\)) having orthonormal columns and \(\mathbf{D}\) diagonal with \(d_1 \ge \dots \ge d_r > 0\). Then \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{D}^2\mathbf{V}^\top\): the columns of \(\mathbf{V}\) are its eigenvectors and the \(d_j^2\) its non-zero eigenvalues.








NoteTheorem C.14 — Ridge regression in SVD coordinates



With \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\top\), the ridge fit is \[
\hat{\mathbf{y}}_\lambda = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} = \sum_j \mathbf{u}_j\,\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda}\,\mathbf{u}_j^\top\mathbf{y} .
\] For \(\lambda = 0\) this is the least-squares projection. The effective degrees of freedom are \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}_\lambda) = \sum_j d_j^2/(d_j^2 + \lambda)\).


Proof. \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{D}^2 + \lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{V}^\top\) (for \(p \le n\) with full rank, \(\mathbf{V}\) square), whose inverse is \(\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{D}^2 + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{V}^\top\). Multiply out: \(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{D}^2 + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{U}^\top = \mathbf{U}\,\mathbf{D}^2(\mathbf{D}^2 + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\,\mathbf{U}^\top\). \(\square\)

Xs <- scale(mtcars[, c("wt", "hp", "disp")]); yc <- mtcars$mpg - mean(mtcars$mpg)
s  <- svd(Xs); lambda <- 5
H_ridge <- Xs %*% solve(t(Xs) %*% Xs + lambda * diag(3)) %*% t(Xs)
c(df_trace = sum(diag(H_ridge)), df_svd = sum(s$d^2 / (s$d^2 + lambda)))

#> df_trace   df_svd 
#> 1.973492 1.973492
